Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 24, verse 27:

"Until you seek permission (tasta'nisu)" has two meanings. The first is that it derives from *al-istiktsas* (seeking companionship or familiarity), which is the opposite of *al-istiwhash* (feeling alienated). Someone who knocks on another's door does not know whether he will be admitted, so he is like one who feels uneasy because the situation is hidden from him. When he is given permission, he feels at ease. The meaning, then, is: "until you are given permission," as in His saying: ﴿Do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless permission is given to you﴾ (33:53). This is a case of *kināya* (allusion or metonymy, a term meaning speaking indirectly) and *irdāf* (concomitance, where one thing implies another), because this kind of being at ease follows upon permission. So the consequence is placed in the position of the permission itself. The second meaning is that it derives from *al-istiknās* (seeking information and making things clear): the form *istif'āl* from *anisa al-shay'* when he saw it plainly and openly. The meaning is "until you seek information and make the situation clear: is entry wanted or not?" From this come the expressions "Istanis, do you see anyone?" and "I looked, but I saw no one," meaning, "I recognised and sought information." From this is the verse of al-Nabigha:

*"As if my saddle, when the day had passed (zāl) over us at Dhu al-Jalil, was on a lone wild ass, one who looks ahead."*

Al-Nabigha describes his camel as being like a wild ass that runs swiftly out of fear of what it has seen. Al-Asma'i said: "*Zāl al-nahār* means the day reached its midpoint, and perhaps this is because the sun left the middle of the sky." It is also possible that the meaning is that it passed and only a little of it remained, as is the more obvious sense when *zawāl* is attributed to *al-nahār*. *Banā* means "over us." It is also possible that the *bā'* expresses accompaniment. *Al-Jalīl* is a tree with fronds like palm fronds. *Dhū al-Jalīl* is a place. *Al-mustanis* is one who raises his head to see whether there is a person. It is also said that he is one who fears company. "*Istanastu bi-l-shay'*" means my heart became settled with it. "*Istanastu*" means I sought information, looked closely, and was wary of anyone there. *Al-wahd* means alone, solitary; a person is *wahīd*. *Wahd* in the forms *ẓarf*, *sabab* and *ḥadhar* means he was alone, meaning the rider was on that wild ass and not on a camel, because of its swiftness, like the wild ass.

It is also possible that it derives from *al-ins* (human beings), meaning that one finds out whether there is a human being present. From Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him, we said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is *al-istiʾnās*?" He said: "A man speaks with a *tasbīḥa* (saying Subhan Allah), a *takbīr* (saying Allahu Akbar), and a *taḥmīda* (saying al-hamdu lillah), and clears his throat, so that the people of the house are alerted." *Al-taslīm* is that he says: "Peace be upon you. May I enter?" three times. If he is given permission, well and good; otherwise he returns. From Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, that he came to the door of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "Peace be upon you. May I enter?" He said it three times, then returned and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: The seeking of permission is three times." A man asked permission to enter upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "May I come in?" The Prophet ﷺ said to a woman called Rawda: "Go to this man and teach him, for he does not know how to ask permission. Tell him to say: 'Peace be upon you. May I enter?'" The man heard her and said it, and he said: "Enter." [Ibn Abi Shayba narrated it from the transmission of Sufyan al-Sammān: I heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr, but he did not name Rawda; he said in it: "And he said to his servant."]

The people of the Jahiliyya used to say, when a man entered a house other than his own: "Good morning to you, good evening to you," and then he would enter. Thus a man might find himself with his wife under one blanket. Allah forbade that and taught what is better and more beautiful. How many doors of religion are, in people's eyes, like an abrogated law, which they have abandoned in practice! The matter of seeking permission is one of these. You are in your house, and the door suddenly bursts open upon you with someone, without seeking permission or any greeting, whether of Islam or of the Jahiliyya, and he is one who has heard what Allah revealed about it and what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said. But where is the attentive ear? [Note: "idhā ra'afa 'alayka al-bāb" — in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, *ra'afa al-rajul* means blood came out of his nose, and *ra'afa al-faras* means it outran and went ahead; so the usage here is metaphorical, by way of comparison. (Ibn Qutayba's? marked (ʿ).]

In the recitation of Abdullah: "until you greet its people and seek permission." From Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: it is only "until you seek permission," but the scribe erred. This report is not to be relied upon. In the recitation of Ubayy: "until you seek permission." ﴿That is the seeking of permission and the greeting; it is better for you than the greeting of the Jahiliyya.﴾ *Al-damūr* is entering without permission. Its derivation is from *al-damār*, which is destruction, as if its doer is ruined by the magnitude of what he has committed. In a hadith: "Whoever his eye outruns his seeking permission has been ruined (damar)." [Al-Tabarani narrated it through Abu al-Safr from Yazid ibn Shurayh from Abu Umama with the wording: "Whoever puts his eye into a house without the permission of its people has ruined it." Also al-Harbi in *al-Gharīb* from the hadith of Thawr ibn Yazid from Yazid ibn Shurayh from Abu Ḥayy al-Mu'adhdhin from Abu Hurayra with the wording: "It is not lawful for a Muslim to look into a house until he seeks permission; if he does, he has ruined (damar)." Abu Ubayda said in *Gharīb al-Ḥadīth*: Hushaym narrated to us from Mansur ibn al-Hasan with its wording as a mursal report; al-Kisa'i said: "damar" with light emphasis means entered without permission.]

It is also narrated that a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "May I seek permission to enter upon my mother?" He said: "Yes." He said: "She has no servant but me; should I seek permission to enter upon her every time I enter?" He said: "Would you like to see her naked?" The man said: "No." He said: "Then seek permission." [Abu Dawud narrated it in *al-Marāsīl* from the hadith of Ata' ibn Yasar, "that a man asked," and mentioned it as a mursal; it is in the *Muwatta'* from Safwan ibn Sulaym from Ata'. Al-Tabari cited it through Ziyad ibn Sa'd from Ata' also as a mursal; Ibn Abi Shayba in *al-Nikāḥ* said: Ibn Uyayna narrated to us from Zayd ibn Aslam, and mentioned it as a mursal.]

﴿That is better for you; perhaps you will remember.﴾ That is, it has been revealed to you; or it was said to you, so that you would remember, take admonition, and act upon what you were commanded concerning the matter of seeking permission.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 24, verse 28:

It may mean: "But if you do not find anyone in it who gives permission, then do not enter it, and wait until someone gives you permission." And it may mean: "But if you do not find anyone in it of its people, and you have a need in it, then do not enter it except with the permission of its people." That is because seeking permission (istidhan) was not prescribed merely so that the onlooker does not see the private parts of another, nor so that his eye does not hasten to what it is not lawful to look at. Rather, it was prescribed so that one does not come upon the states which people ordinarily conceal from others and guard against anyone's gaining knowledge of them. Also, because it is a disposal of another's property, it must be with his consent; otherwise it resembles usurpation and domination.

﴿Then return﴾: that is, do not persist in demanding permission, do not press to ease the veil, and do not stand at the doors waiting, for this brings about resentment and taints people's hearts, especially if they are people of dignity and trained in good manners. And when this is forbidden because it leads to resentment, it is obligatory to refrain from everything that leads to it: knocking on the door violently, calling out to the householder loudly, and other things that fall under the habits of those of the majority of people who have not been refined.

It is reported from Abu 'Ubayd: "I never knocked on a door of a scholar at all." And the story of the Banu Asad suffices as a deterrent, along with what was revealed concerning it: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers, most of them do not understand﴾.

If you say: Is it valid that the meaning be: "And if you are not given permission and you are told to return, then comply, and do not enter despite their dislike"? I say: Since the prohibition of entering in the absence of permission alone has been affirmed, whether the people of the house are present or absent, there remains no doubt that it is forbidden when the command to return is added to the absence of permission.

If you say: Then what if an affair arises in a house, such as a fire, the intrusion of a thief, or the appearance of an evil that must be denounced? I say: That is excepted by evidence; that is, ﴿returning is purer for you and more pure﴾, because of what it contains of the soundness of hearts and distance from suspicion. Or ﴿more beneficial and more productive of good﴾.

Then He threatened those addressed with this, saying that He knows what they do and what they leave undone of what they were addressed with, so He will repay them for it.

He excepted from the houses for which seeking permission to enter is required those that are not inhabited, such as the inns (funduq), namely the caravanserais (khanat), the lodgings (rubut), and the shops of merchants. And "al-mata'" (benefit) means the advantage, such as sheltering from heat and cold, lodging travelers and goods, and buying and selling. It is narrated that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah the Exalted has revealed a verse to you concerning seeking permission, and we are engaged in trade and we stay in these caravanserais. Should we not enter them except with permission?" [[لم أجده]] Then it was revealed. It was also said: the ruined dwellings (kharabat) where one relieves oneself. And "al-mata'" means relieving oneself. ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾ is a warning to those who enter ruined dwellings and empty houses that are free of people of suspicion.

Min is used partially (lil-tab'id, "for partiality"), and the intended meaning is lowering the gaze from what is forbidden and restricting it to what is permitted. Al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat) allowed that it could be superfluous (muzidah, "an added particle"), but Sibawayh (Sibawayh, the grammarian) rejected this.

If you ask: why was it introduced with lowering the gaze, but not with guarding the private parts?

I answer: it indicates that the matter of looking is broader. Do you not see that there is no harm in looking at the hair, chests, breasts, upper arms, shins and feet of mahram relatives, and likewise at the female slaves offered for sale? As for a non-mahram woman, one may look at her face, hands and feet according to one of the two reports. As for the matter of the private parts, it is restricted: it is enough of a distinction that looking was permitted except in what was excepted from it, while intercourse was prohibited except in what was excepted from it.

It is also possible that what is meant, along with guarding them from resorting to what is not lawful, is guarding them from exposing them. Ibn Zayd said: "Every mention of guarding the private parts in the Qur'an refers to illicit sexual intercourse (zina), except this one, for by it he meant concealment (al-istitar)."

Then He informed that He is Aware (Khabir) of their deeds and their states: how do they direct their gazes, and how do they deal with the rest of their senses and limbs? So they, having come to know this, should be mindful of Him and wary of Him in every movement and stillness.

Women are likewise commanded to lower their gaze. It is not permitted for a woman to look at a non-mahram man at anything from below his navel to his knee. If she feels desire, she must lower her gaze entirely. She may look at a woman only at the same parts.

Lowering her gaze from non-mahram men altogether is better and more fitting for her. This includes the hadith of Ibn Umm Maktum, narrated from Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Maymuna was with him. Ibn Umm Maktum came in, and that was after we had been commanded to observe the hijab. He entered upon us and said: 'Veil yourselves.' We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is he not blind and unable to see?' He said: 'Are you two blind? Do you not see him?'" [[Recorded by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, Ahmad, Ishaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani, all through a narration from Bunhan, the scribe of Umm Salama, from her. al-Nasa'i said: "We know of no one who narrated from Bunhan except al-Zuhri." Ishaq said in his Musnad: Yahya ibn Adam informed us, Mughal narrated to us from Yunus, from al-Zuhri, from Nahhan, from Umm Salama, who said: "Ibn Umm Maktum asked permission to enter while I and Zaynab were with him..." – the hadith. Mandal is weak; he differed in mentioning Zaynab instead of Maymuna.]]

If you ask: why did He put the lowering of the gaze before guarding the private parts? I say: because looking is the messenger of adultery and the guide to immorality, and the trial in it is greater and more frequent, and one can hardly guard against it.

Adornment (al-zina) is what a woman adorns herself with, whether jewelry, kohl or dye. What is visible of it, such as the ring, the fatkha [[On the phrase "al-fatkha" in al-Sihah: the fatkha, with a vowel on the first letter, is a silver ring without a stone. If it has a stone, it is a khatim (ring). Women sometimes wear it on their toe. Also in it: "al-iklil" is a headband-like ornament decorated with jewels, and the crown is called iklil. (Editor's note: ʿ)]], kohl and dye, may be shown to non-mahram men without any harm. What is hidden, such as the bracelet, anklet, armlet, necklace, iklil, wishah, and earring, may be shown only to the people mentioned.

Mentioning the adornment rather than the places where it is worn is for emphasis on the command to guard and conceal, because these adornments are located on parts of the body that may not be looked at by anyone other than those mentioned. These are the forearm, shin, upper arm, neck, head, chest and ear. He prohibited the display of the adornments themselves, so that it is known that if looking at them is not permitted because they touch those places, then since looking at the adornments without touching those places is clearly permitted, looking at the places themselves is all the more firmly forbidden, and their prohibition is established, and it shows that women must be careful in covering them and must fear Allah in uncovering them. [[Mahmud said: "The meaning is a prohibition on displaying the places of adornment. The prohibition is not directly on displaying the adornment itself, but the adornment is used as a metaphor for displaying its places, by way of the more appropriate reading." Ahmad said: His saying, Exalted is He, after that: ﴿and that they should not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known﴾, confirms that displaying the adornment itself is directly intended by the prohibition, because He prohibited what is a means to it specifically. Stamping the feet is forbidden only because it reveals that a woman has adornment even if it is not shown, let alone its places. And Allah knows best.]]

If you say: what do you say about al-qarameel [[On "al-qarameel" in al-Sihah: it is what a woman fastens in her hair. (Editor's note: ʿ)]]: is it permitted for these men to look at it? I say: yes. If you say: is its place not the back, and is it not forbidden for them to look at her back and belly, and sometimes the hair is loose so that the qarameel falls on what lies opposite the area below the navel? I say: the matter is as you said, but the ruling on the qarameel differs from that of the other jewelry, because it is worn only over clothing. Looking at a garment that lies over the back and belly is permitted for non-mahram men, let alone for these people, unless it is so thin that it shows what is beneath, in which case looking at it is not permitted, and so it is not permitted to look at the qarameel lying upon it.

If you say: what is meant by the place of adornment: is it that entire limb, or only the portion that the adornment touches? I say: the correct view is that it is the entire limb, just as I explained the places of hidden adornment. Likewise the places of visible adornment: the face is the place of kohl on the eyes, and of dye (wasma) on the eyebrows and mustache, and of ghumra on the cheeks; the palm and the foot are the places of the ring, the fatkha and henna dye. [[On "wasma" in al-Sihah: wasma, with a kasra on the sin, is 'izlam, a dye used for coloring; its sukun is also a dialect form. Also: 'izlam is a plant used for dyeing. Also: ghumra is a cosmetic paste made from saffron. (Editor's note: ʿ)]]

If you ask: why was leniency granted generally regarding visible adornment? I say: because concealing it causes hardship, for a woman cannot avoid handling things with her hands, and needs to uncover her face, especially in testimony, litigation and marriage, and she is compelled to walk in the streets with her feet exposed, particularly poor women. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿except what is apparent of it﴾, that is, except what custom and nature have made customary to be visible, and the basic principle is that it is visible. Leniency was granted for hidden adornment only regarding those mentioned, because they are the ones with whom there is an urgent need to mix and associate, and because there is little expectation of temptation from them, and because human nature is averse to touching close relatives. A woman needs their company while traveling for dismounting, mounting and other matters.

Their collars were wide, so their necks and chests and what surrounds them would show, and they used to let the khimar fall behind their backs, leaving those areas uncovered. So they were commanded to let it fall in front of them until they covered them. It is permissible for "al-juyub" (collars) to mean the chests, by naming a thing after what is adjacent to and connected with it. From this come the expressions "nasih al-jayb" (a sincere-breasted one) and your saying: "I struck with her khimar over her collar," just as you would say: "I struck with my hand on the wall," when you place it upon it. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "I have not seen women better than the women of the Ansar. When this verse was revealed, each of them rose to her murut [[On "al-murt" in al-Sihah: it is a woolen or silk cloak worn as a wrap. Also: "murt murhal" is a silk wrapper with designs. (Editor's note: ʿ)]], the striped one, tore a strip from it and covered herself with it, so that on their heads it was as if there were crows."

It was read "juyubihinna" with a kasra on the jim for the sake of the ya'. Likewise, regarding ﴿houses other than your own﴾, it was said regarding "their women": they are believing women, because it is not permitted for a believing woman to strip before a polytheist or a People of the Book. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The apparent meaning is that by "their women" is meant those who are in their company and service, whether free women or slave women or women in general, all of whom are equal in permitting one another to look at each other. It was also said: "what their right hands possess" means both male and female slaves together. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, permitted her male slave to look at her, and said to Dhakwan: "When you place me in the grave and leave, you are free." [[This is a composite of two reports. The first: al-Bayhaqi recorded it through 'Amr ibn Maymun from Sulayman ibn Yasar, who said: "I asked permission to enter upon 'A'isha, and she said: 'Sulayman? Come in, for you are a slave as long as one dirham remains owed by you.'" al-Bukhari also reported it from Sulayman. The second was recorded by Ibn Sa'd through Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, that 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "When I am shrouded, buried and anointed, and Dhakwan lowers me into my grave, he is free." 'Abd al-Razzaq recorded it from Ibn Jurayj: Ibn Abi Mulayka informed me that 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "When Abu 'Amr buries me and lowers me into my grave, he is free."]]. Similarly, it is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab the same [[I have not seen it.]]. Then he retracted and said: "Let not the verse of the Light deceive you, for by it is meant only slave women." [[Ibn Abi Shayba recorded it through Tariq from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: "Do not be deceived by the verse: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾; it means only slave women, not male slaves."]] This is the correct view, because a woman's male slave holds the status of a non-mahram man to her, whether he is castrated or intact.

It is narrated from Maysun bint Bahdal al-Kalabiyya that Mu'awiya entered upon her with a eunuch, and she covered her face from him. He said: "He is a eunuch." She said: "O Mu'awiya, do you think that mutilation of him makes lawful what Allah has forbidden?" [[I have not found it. I say: al-Mas'udi mentioned it in Muruj al-Dhahab without a chain of narration. Note: al-Kashshaf has "al-Kalabiyya." The correct form is "al-Kalbiyya" with a sukun on the lam. The story is mentioned by others as "bint Qurza."]]

According to Abu Hanifa, it is not permitted to employ eunuchs, to keep them, or to buy and sell them. No one from the early generations is reported to have kept them. If you say: it is reported that a eunuch was given as a gift to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he accepted him. I say: in matters where the general need is widespread, one accepts only an unambiguous hadith. If it is authentic, perhaps he accepted him in order to free him, or for some other reason. [[al-Ibn Sa'd recorded: Muhammad ibn 'Umar informed us, Ya'qub ibn Abi Sa'sa'a narrated to us from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Sa'sa'a, who said: "al-Muqawqis, ruler of Alexandria, sent to the Prophet ﷺ in the seventh year after the Hijra: Mariya and her sister Sirin, a thousand mithqals of gold, twenty garments, a mule, his donkey 'Ufayr, and a eunuch called Ma Yawad. Hatib presented Islam to Mariya, and she and her sister embraced Islam, and then the eunuch embraced Islam afterward." The mention of this eunuch occurs in several hadiths, including a hadith from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

And his saying: "This is weak, and is not accepted in matters of general need, except an unambiguous hadith, if authentic. Perhaps he accepted him in order to free him," end quote. And this has nothing to do with matters of general need.]]

"Ghayr uli al-irba" (those without need): the meaning of "irba" is need. It was said: these are the ones who follow you to get some of your food, and they have no need for women, because they are simple and know nothing of such matters. Or they are righteous elderly men who lower their gaze when with women, or men who are impotent. It was read "ghayri" in the accusative as an exception or as a circumstantial clause, and in the genitive as a qualifier. The singular is placed in the position of the plural because it conveys a genus, and what follows clarifies that the plural is intended. A similar usage is ﴿We bring you forth as a child﴾.

"Lam yazharu" (who have not attained knowledge of) may come from "zahara 'ala al-shay'" meaning "to be acquainted with a thing," that is, they do not know what the private parts are and cannot distinguish them from other parts. Or it may come from "zahara 'ala fulan" meaning "to overpower someone," and "zahara 'ala al-Qur'an" meaning "to master it and be able to recite it," that is, they have not reached the ability to engage in intercourse. It was read "'awrat" (private parts), which is the dialect of Hudhayl.

If you ask: why did Allah not mention paternal and maternal uncles? It was said to al-Sha'bi about that, and he said: "So that the uncle does not describe her to his son, and the maternal uncle likewise." The meaning is that the rest of the relatives share mahram status with the father and son, except the paternal and maternal uncles and their sons. So if the father sees her, he may describe her to his son, though the son is not a mahram to her, and his mental picture of her from the description brings him close to looking at her. This is also one of the eloquent indications of the obligation on women to be careful in covering themselves.

A woman used to strike the ground with her foot so that her anklet would jingle, so that it would be known that she wore an anklet. It was also said: she would strike one foot against the other so that it would be known that she wore two anklets. When they were forbidden to make the sound of jewelry known, after being forbidden to display the jewelry itself, it is understood that the prohibition on displaying the places of jewelry is stronger and stronger still. The commands and prohibitions of Allah in every matter are such that a weak servant can hardly observe them, even if he restrains himself and strives, and he is not free from some shortcoming that befalls him. Therefore He instructed all the believers to repent and seek forgiveness, and to hope for success if they repent and seek forgiveness. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Repent of what you used to do in the Jahiliyya, so that you may be successful in this world and the Hereafter."

If you ask: repentance was already valid through Islam, and Islam erases what came before it, so what is the meaning of this repentance? I say: by it is meant what the scholars say: whoever commits a sin and then repents of it must renew repentance from it whenever he remembers it, because he must continue in his remorse and resolve until he meets his Lord.

It was read "ayyuhal-mu'minun" with a damma on the ha'. Its basis is that it was originally fatha because it came before the alif. When the alif was dropped because of two consecutive unvocalized letters, its vowel was made to follow the vowel of the letter before it.

**al-Ayāmā wa-al-yatāmā** (the unmarried and the orphans): their original forms were *ayāʾim* and *yatāʾim*, and the letters were transposed. *Al-ayyim* applies to both men and women. One says *āma*, *āmat*, and *ta'ayyama* when a man or a woman does not marry, whether virgin or previously married. He said:

*"If you marry, I will marry; and if you remain unmarried, I too will remain unmarried, even though I am younger than you and in the prime of youth."*

[[*Āma al-rajulu* (with the long vowel) and *al-mar'a*. *Ta'ayyama* means that a man or woman does not marry, whether virgin or previously married. He is saying to his beloved: if you marry, I will marry, and if you do not marry, I will not marry. The clause "wa-in kuntu afta minkum" is a parenthetical interjection. *Al-afta* means the one who is more youthful and more vigorous. He used the plural masculine pronoun to show honour, and the raising of the imperfect verb after the conditional particle, as here, is rare; he probably did it for the sake of the rhyme.]]

And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) [[I have not found it]]: "O Allah, we seek refuge in You from *al-ʿayma* (a craving for milk), *al-ghayma* (thirst and burning of the belly), *al-ayma* (widowhood), *al-kazm* and *al-qaram*." [[In the *Sihah* (of al-Jawhari), *al-ʿayma* is the craving for milk. And there: *al-ghaym* is thirst and burning of the belly, which indicates that *al-ghayma* is the single instance of that. And there: *al-ayāmā* are those men and women who have no spouses. *Āmat al-mar'a* from her husband, *tay'im ayma*. And there: *kazama al-shay'* with its front part, that is, he broke it and extracted what was in it. And there: *qarama al-ṣabī wa-al-bahm qaraman*, meaning weak eating at the very beginning of eating. *Al-qaram*, with a vowel on the *r*, means intense desire for meat. In one narration the word is *al-qadhm* with a *dh* in place of the *r*. In the *Sihah*: *al-qadhm*, on the pattern of *al-hajf*, means severe. And there also: *al-hajf* of the ostriches and of people is the one who is coarse and heavy. Al-Kumayt said:

"He is the most fearless and the most sharp-tongued among us in courage, and among those who oppose him he is the heavy, coarse one."

The metre does not stand unless the *fāʾ* is doubled. And there, *al-hawwās* means the lion.]] The meaning is: marry off those among you who are unmarried, free men and free women, and those among your male and female slaves who are righteous. [[And it is read: "from your slaves" (*ʿabīdikum*).]] This command is for recommendation (*al-nadb*, a recommended act) because it is known that marriage is a recommended matter. [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is a command, and what is meant by it is recommendation. Then he mentioned hadiths that indicate this, and included in them his saying, peace be upon him: 'Whoever finds the means to marry and does not marry is not of us.'" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "Interpreting this as obligation would be more appropriate. But similar wording has been reported regarding abandoning sunnas many times, and it seems the meaning is: whoever does not follow our sunna. Moreover, it has been reported regarding obligatory matters, such as his saying: 'Whoever cheats us is not of us,' and avoiding deception is obligatory; and 'Whoever draws a weapon during civil strife is not of us,' and similar examples are numerous."]] It may be obligatory on the guardians when the woman requests it. And according to the literalists (*ahl al-zawāhir*, those who follow the apparent meaning of texts), marriage is obligatory. Among what indicates that it is recommended is his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever loves my *fiṭra* (natural disposition), let him follow my sunna, and it is marriage." [[ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated it from the narration of ʿUbayd ibn Saʿīd who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said..." and mentioned it as a *mursal* (a hadith whose chain omits the Companion). Abū Yaʿlā narrated it through this same route, as though he thought that ʿUbayd ibn Saʿīd had companionship (with the Prophet). Ibn ʿAdī has, from the narration of Abū Ḥarra Wāṣil ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from al-Ḥasan, from Abū Hurayra, the wording: "Whoever loves my *fiṭra*, let him certainly follow my sunna, and indeed among my sunna is marriage."]] And from him, peace be upon him: "Whoever has the means to marry and does not marry is not of us." [[Abū Dāwūd in *al-Marāsīl*, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, al-Dārimī, al-Ṭabarānī, ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn Abī Shayba all narrated it through the narration of Abū al-Mufallis from Abū Najīḥ, raised to the Prophet: "Whoever is able to marry and does not marry is not of us." al-Thaʿlabī narrated it through this route with the wording of the author. Ibn Rāhawayh said: "Some narrated it from Ibn Jurayj, from Abū al-Mufallis, from Abū Najīḥ ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasa who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said this is a mistake, and Abū Najīḥ is not ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasa. It has been narrated by al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Usāma in his *Musnad*, from al-Ḥakam ibn Mūsā, from al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from Ibn Jurayj: "Abū al-Mufallis narrated to me: I heard Abū Najīḥ al-Sulamī say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say..." and he mentioned something similar.]] And from him, peace be upon him: "When one of you marries, his devil cries out: 'Woe to him! This son of Adam has protected two-thirds of his religion from me.'" [[Abū Yaʿlā and al-Ṭabarānī in *al-Awsat*, and al-Thaʿlabī, narrated it through the narration of Ṣāliḥ, client of al-Tawʾama, from Jābir. And from some of them, from Abū Hurayra instead of Jābir. In its chain is Khālid ibn Ismāʿīl al-Makhzūmī, who is *matrūk* (abandoned, i.e., weak).]] And from him, peace be upon him: "O ʿIyāḍ, do not marry an old woman or a barren one, for I will be proud of (my) numbers." [[al-Ḥākim and al-Thaʿlabī narrated it through the narration of Muʿāwiya ibn Yaḥyā, from Yaḥyā ibn Jābir, from Jubayr ibn Muʿmar, from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ghanm al-Ashʿarī. Muʿāwiya is weak. The author said: "The hadiths from the Prophet (ﷺ) and the reports on this subject are numerous." Among them is the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) in the two *Ṣaḥīḥs* (of al-Bukhārī and Muslim): "Some people among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) asked his wives about his worship in private. Some of them said: I will not eat meat. Some said: I will not marry women... ," and in it: "But I fast and break my fast, I pray and sleep, I eat meat and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my sunna is not of me." Among them is the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him): "O assembly of youth, whoever among you is able to marry (*al-bāʾa*, marriage or the means of it), let him marry," agreed upon, and it was mentioned in *al-Māʾida*. And the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "He used to command marriage and forbid celibacy (*al-tabattul*)," narrated by Ibn Ḥibbān. And the hadith: "Marry, multiply and reproduce, for I will boast of you before the nations," has many routes in the *Sunan* and elsewhere. And the hadith of ʿAṭiyya ibn Bishr in the story of ʿUkkāf ibn Wadāʿa al-Hilālī, urging marriage, in which is: "Indeed the worst of you are your unmarried ones." Isḥāq narrated it in his *Musnad*: Nuḍayya informed us, from Muʿāwiya ibn Yaḥyā al-Ṣadafī, that he narrated to him from Sulaymān ibn Mūsā, from Makḥūl, from Ghuḍayf ibn al-Ḥārith, from ʿAṭiyya ibn Bishr, at length. al-Ṭabarānī narrated it in *Musnad al-Shāmiyyīn* through Ibn ʿUtba, from Burd ibn Sinān, from Makḥūl, from ʿAṭiyya ibn Bishr, without mentioning Ghuḍayf. Aḥmad said: ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated to us from Muḥammad ibn Rāshid, from Makḥūl, from Abū Dharr, and mentioned something similar. And among them is the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever marries has completed half of faith, so let him fear Allah regarding the other half." Al-Ṭabarānī narrated it in *al-Awsat*, and its chain is very weak. The rest of it will come later.]] The hadiths on this subject from the Prophet (ﷺ) and the reports are numerous. Sometimes abandoning it is obligatory, when it leads to disobedience or harm. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When there come upon my community a hundred and eighty years, celibacy, seclusion, and monasticism on the mountaintops become permissible for them." [[al-Bayhaqī and al-Thaʿlabī narrated it from a hadith of Ibn Masʿūd. In its chain is Sulaymān ibn ʿĪsā al-Khurāsānī, who is a liar. Through his route Ibn al-Jawzī narrated it in *al-Mawḍūʿāt* (the fabricated hadiths), but it has another route. ʿAlī ibn Maʿbad narrated it in *Kitāb al-Ṭāʿa wa-al-Maʿṣiya* from al-Ḥasan ibn Wāqid al-Ḥanafī, who said: I think it is from the hadith of Bahz ibn Ḥakīm, and he mentioned it, and it is connected.]] And in a hadith: "A time will come upon people when livelihood cannot be obtained except through disobedience. When that time comes, celibacy becomes permissible." [[ʿAlī ibn Maʿbad narrated in *al-Ṭāʿa wa-al-Maʿṣiya*, from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubārak, from Mubārak ibn Faḍāla, from al-Ḥasan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A time will come upon people when the one who holds to his religion will not be safe in it except by fleeing with his religion from peak to peak and from rock to rock. When that time comes, celibacy becomes permissible." It was asked: "How does celibacy become permissible?" and he mentioned a long hadith. al-Khaṭṭābī connected it in *al-ʿUzla*, through the route of al-Saʿrā ibn Yaḥyā, from al-Ḥasan, from Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, from ʿAbd Allah. In its chain is Muḥammad ibn Yūnus al-Kudaymī, who is weak.]]

If you say: why did He single out the righteous? I say: so that their religion is protected and their righteousness is preserved for them. Also, the righteous among the slaves are those whose masters are compassionate toward them and treat them as children in favour and affection, so they are likely to be recommended and cared for, and their recommendation is likely to be accepted. As for the corrupt among them, their situation with their masters is the opposite. Or the meaning of righteousness is: fulfilling the rights of marriage. The condition of Allah should not be forgotten in this promise and its like, which is His will. [[His speech resumes. He said: "The condition of wisdom and benefit should not be forgotten." He cited as evidence His saying: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills﴾ (9:28). Ahmad said: His inclination toward a corrupt belief prevents him from being correct, for his belief is that Allah is obliged to observe benefits. Hence he made the condition of wisdom and benefit a narrow limit on the bounty of Allah. Then he cited as evidence something that is evidence against him and not for him, for the statement of Allah in the other verse, "if He wills," indicates that the occurrence of wealth is conditional on will alone. This is the belief of the People of Truth. So the stipulation of wisdom falls out of the place of inference. Exalted is the Lord of lords above being obligated. But it is necessary to draw attention to a point for which there is a need to point it out, so that its benefit may be general and its impact great, if Allah wills. That is: if we establish that there is an omitted condition, it is necessary to estimate it, because the truthfulness of the report requires it. For if we believed that Allah makes every married person rich without qualification, while we see many whose poverty continued after marriage, or even increased, then the promise would be broken, and Allah is exalted above that. So it is established that there is a necessity to estimate a condition in order to reconcile the promise with reality. The Qadariyya (the determinists) say: the meaning is, "if wisdom requires it." So everyone whom Allah does not enrich by the effect of marriage is someone whose enrichment wisdom does not require. We have refuted that this condition is the estimated one, and we have insisted that the estimated condition is the condition of will, as appears in the other verse. Then every person who becomes rich through marriage, that is because Allah did not will his wealth. One might say: if will is what counts in the wealth of the married person, then it is also what counts in the wealth of the single person. So what is the point of linking the promise of wealth to marriage, when the situation of the one who marries is divided in wealth according to will: some are made rich by it and some remain poor, just as the situation of one who does not marry is likewise divided? This is not like the affirmation of the condition of will in forgiveness for the sinful monotheist, for the promise there is linked to monotheism, and even though it is also linked to will, since the non-monotheist will certainly not be forgiven by Allah, you cannot say: the non-married person will certainly not be made rich by Allah, because reality contradicts it. The answer, and with Allah is success: the benefit of linking wealth to marriage is that people's natures have been set to rest upon causes and rely on them, and to be heedless of the Causer, the Majestic and Exalted. So much so that the illusion dominated the intellect, and it imagined that a large number of dependants is a cause that necessarily produces poverty, and that their absence is a cause that necessarily produces the accumulation of wealth, even though neither of these two causes influences what the illusion has linked to them. So it was intended to uproot this illusion established in human nature, by announcing that Allah may increase wealth and make it grow despite a large number of dependants, which in illusions is a cause of the exhaustion of wealth. And He may decree poverty despite their absence, which in illusions is a cause of multiplication. Reality witnesses to this, without doubt. This clearly shows that the causes which humans imagine to be inseparably linked to their effects are not as they suppose. Rather, wealth and poverty are decreed by the Causer of causes, and their decree depends on no one but a specific will. Then the wise and alert person does not shy away from marriage, because it is established for him that it has no effect on poverty, and that Allah does not prevent it from enriching him. Nor does abstention from marriage for the sake of abundance affect him, because it is established that it has no effect on that, and that no obstacle prevents Allah from making him poor. And if the servant takes a cause, he should not look to it, but to the will of Allah, exalted. So the meaning of His saying then, ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾ (24:32), is that marriage does not prevent them from wealth from the bounty of Allah. He expressed the negation of its being an obstacle to wealth by its existence alongside it. The obstruction is not nullified by the existence of what was imagined to be obstructed alongside what was imagined to be an obstacle, even in one form or another, as a consequence of that. Of this type is His saying: ﴿So when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land﴾ (62:10). The apparent meaning of the command is to request dispersal at the conclusion of prayer, and this is not the literal intent. Rather the purpose is to establish the removal of the obstacle, which is prayer, and to show that once prayer is concluded there is no obstacle. So he expressed the negation of the obstacle by dispersal, in a way that conveys the request for dispersal, for emphasis in establishing the meaning for the hearer, and Allah knows best. Reflect on this section and take it as a support where there is need for it.]], and the Wise does not will except what wisdom requires and what is beneficial. [[His saying: "except what wisdom requires and what is beneficial" seems to be based on the view that it is obligatory for Allah to do what is good, which is the position of the Muʿtazila (the rationalists). According to Ahl al-Sunna: nothing is obligatory upon Allah. (Ibn al-Munayyir).]] Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out, and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ (65:2–3). The condition has been stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills. Indeed Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ (9:28). Whoever does not forget this condition will not stand objecting that a single man who was rich became poor through marriage, or that a sinner who repented and feared Allah had some wealth which then vanished and he became a poor man.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Seek provision through marriage." [[al-Thaʿlabī narrated it from the narration of Muslim ibn Khālid, and Ibn Mardawayh from the narration of Abū al-Sāʾib Salām ibn Janāda, from Abū Usāma, from Hishām, from his father, from ʿĀʾisha, raised: "Marry women, for they bring wealth." al-Ḥākim said: Salām alone narrated it, and he is trustworthy. al-Bazzār and al-Dāraqutnī, and others besides Salām, narrate it as a *mursal*. That is what they said, and it is as they said. Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba narrated it from Abū Usāma without mentioning ʿĀʾisha. Likewise Abū Dāwūd in *al-Marāsīl* narrated it from Ibn al-Tawʾama, from Abū Usāma. Abū al-Qāsim Ḥamza ibn Yūsuf narrated it in *Tārīkh Jurjān* through the narration of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAllawān, from Hishām, connected. al-Ḥusayn is accused of lying. *Note*: The one who took it out thought that this refutes the statements of al-Bazzār and al-Dāraqutnī. That is not as he thought, because he said: "ʿAbd al-Mumin al-ʿAṭṭār has followed him," and he also said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Nājiya has followed him." As for the first, the one who followed is actually al-Ḥusayn, the teacher of ʿAbd al-Mumin, and we have said he is worth nothing. As for the second, Ibn Nājiya narrated it only from Abū al-Sāʾib himself, so the solitary transmission of Abū al-Sāʾib in connecting it, among the trustworthy, is clear. As for al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAllawān, his following adds nothing because of his weakness.]] And a man complained to him of need, so he said [[al-Thaʿlabī narrated it from the narration of al-Dāraqutnī, from Abū ʿAjlān: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and complained to him of need..." the hadith.]]: "Hold to *al-bāʾa* (marriage)." [[His saying: "Hold to *al-bāʾa*." In the *Sihah* marriage is called *bāʾ* and *bāʾa*, because a man *yatabawwaʾu* (settles, takes a place) from his family, that is, he gains access to them, as he settles in his house. Also there: *al-rāziḥ* from camels, the one who perishes from emaciation. If it is specific to camels, it may be extended to others. (Ibn al-Munayyir).]]

And from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): "I am amazed at the one who does not seek wealth through *al-bāʾa* (marriage)." [[Hishām ibn Ḥassān narrated it from al-Ḥasan, from ʿUmar, similarly.]] And there was among us a man in a poor condition. Then I saw him years later, and his situation had improved and become good. I asked him, and he said: "I was at the beginning of my affair as you know, and that was before I was blessed with a child. When I was blessed with my first son, I began to be relieved of poverty. When a second son was born to me, I increased in goodness. When we became three, Allah poured goodness upon me in abundance, and I have become what you see." ﴿And Allah is All-Embracing﴾, that is, the Rich, possessor of vastness, whom the enrichment of creatures does not diminish. [[His saying: "does not diminish" means does not reduce. (Ibn al-Munayyir).]] But He is ﴿Knowing﴾, who extends provision to whom He wills and measures it.

And let those who find no means of marriage keep themselves chaste (wal-yastaʿfif), and strive for chastity and restrain the soul (ẓalf al-nafs) [[His words "restrain the soul" (ẓalf al-nafs): in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "ẓalafa nafsahu ʿan al-shayʾ" means he restrained it from the thing. "Ẓalifat nafsī ʿan kadhā" (with kasra) means I refrained. (ʿ)]], as if the one who seeks chastity is asking his soul for chastity and compelling it toward it, ﴿who find no means of marriage﴾, that is, no ability to marry. It is also permissible that by marriage (nikāḥ) is meant the wealth with which one marries, ﴿until Allah enriches them﴾ by His bounty. This is an encouragement for those who seek chastity and a preliminary promise of Allah's favour to them through riches, so that awaiting and hoping for it becomes a kindness to them in their chastity and a strengthening of their hearts, and so that it becomes clear that His favour is more fitting for their being kept chaste and nearer to the righteous. How excellent is the ordering of these commands: He first commanded what protects from temptation and keeps one away from committing sin, which is lowering the gaze; then marriage, by which religion is protected and self-sufficiency through the lawful is attained instead of the unlawful; then compelling the soul that commands to evil and turning it away from aspiring to desire when unable to marry, until one is granted the capacity for it.

﴿And those who seek a deed of manumission﴾ is in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), or in the accusative by a hidden verb that the following word explains: ﴿then write it for them﴾, as in your saying "Zayd, strike him." The fāʾ entered because the clause carries the sense of a condition. Al-kitāb and al-mukātaba, like al-ʿitāb and al-muʿātaba, mean that a man says to his slave: "I have made a contract of manumission with you for a thousand dirhams, so if he pays it, he is freed." The meaning: I have written for you upon myself that you be freed from me when you have fulfilled the money, and you have written for me upon yourself that you fulfil that. Or: I have written upon you the obligation to pay the money and upon myself the manumission.

According to Abū Ḥanīfa (may Allah be pleased with him), it is permissible whether immediate or deferred, in instalments or not in instalments, because Allah the Exalted did not mention instalments, and by analogy with all other contracts. According to al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him), it is not permissible except deferred and in instalments. It is not permissible in his view to be in a single instalment, because the slave owns nothing, so making the contract immediate prevents the purpose from being achieved, since he cannot pay the sum at once. It is permissible to contract for a small or large amount of money, for service over a known period, or for a known task limited in time, such as digging a well in a specific place of known length and breadth, or building a house whose bricks, plaster and building materials have been shown. If he contracts for his value, it is not permissible. If he pays it, he is freed.

If he contracts with him for a servant [[His words "for a servant" (waṣīf): al-waṣīf is the servant, whether male or female, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]], it is permissible, because the ignorance involved is slight, and the middle course is obligatory. He may not have sexual relations with the female contracted slave. When she pays, she is freed, and her clientage (walāʾ) belongs to her master, because he has given her the earnings which in origin were his. This command is recommendatory according to the majority of scholars. From al-Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him): it is not a binding obligation; if he wishes he may contract, and if he wishes he need not. From ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): it is one of the binding resolutions of Allah. The same is related from Ibn Sīrīn, and it is the view of Dāwūd.

﴿If you know any good in them﴾: ability to pay what they have agreed upon. It was said: trustworthiness and earning. From Salmān (may Allah be pleased with him): a slave of his sought to contract with him, and he said: "Do you have money?" He said: "No." He said: "Do you order me to eat the washings of people's hands?"

﴿And give them﴾ is a command to Muslims, obligatory, to aid the contracted slaves and to give them their share which Allah has appointed for them from the public treasury, as in His saying ﴿and for the captives﴾, according to Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions (may Allah be pleased with them). If you ask: may his master take from what was given to him as charity, if he is rich? I say: Yes. Likewise, if the charity does not cover the whole sum and he is unable to pay the remainder, what the master takes is lawful for him, because he did not take it by reason of the charity but by reason of the contract of manumission, like one who buys charity from a poor man, or inherits it, or is given it as a gift. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Barīrah: "It is a charity for her and a gift for us" [[Agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh), from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) in the course of the narration about the story of Barīrah and her manumission.]]. According to al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him): it is an obligation on the masters to remit for them from the contract money, and if they do not, they are compelled. From ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him): a quarter is to be remitted for him. From Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both): he should be given something from his contract. From ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he contracted with a slave of his called Abū Umayyah, who was the first slave to be contracted in Islam. He brought him the first instalment, and ʿUmar gave it back to him and said: "Use it to help with your contract." He said: "What if I postpone it to the last instalment?" He said: "I fear you will not reach that." [[Ibn Abī Shaybah related it through ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās, except his words "and he was the first slave to be contracted in Islam," which he mentioned at the end as the words of ʿIkrimah. He added: then he recited ﴿and give them of the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾. Ibn Abī Ḥātim related it through Wakīʿ, the teacher of Ibn Abī Shaybah, in the same way.]] According to Abū Ḥanīfa (may Allah be pleased with him), this is recommendatory, and he said: it is a contract of exchange, so one is not compelled to remit, as in sale.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿and give them﴾ is: lend them. It was said: spend on them after they have paid and been freed.

All of this is recommended. It is related that Ḥuwayṭib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā had a slave called al-Ṣabīḥ, who asked his master to contract with him, but he refused, and then this was revealed. The slave-girls of the people of the Jāhiliyyah used to prostitute themselves for their masters, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, the head of the hypocrites, had six slave-girls: Muʿādhah, Musaykah, Umaymah, ʿAmrah, Aroā and Qutaylah, whom he compelled to prostitution and imposed fees upon them. Two of them complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then this was revealed. The words "young man" (fatā) and "young woman" (fatāh) are used as euphemisms for slave and slave-girl. In the hadith: "Let none of you say 'my slave' and 'my slave-girl,' but let him say 'my young man' and 'my young woman'" [[Mentioned previously in al-Kahf.]]. Al-bighāʾ is the verbal noun of al-baghy.

If you ask: why was His saying ﴿if they desire chastity﴾ inserted? I say: because compulsion cannot occur except where desire for chastity is present; an obedient willing one who is prepared for prostitution is not called compelled, nor is his command compulsion. [[Maḥmūd said: "If you ask: why was His saying 'if they desire chastity' inserted? I say: because compulsion occurs only when they desire chastity, and it cannot be conceived otherwise, for otherwise they would be willing." He did not answer with what would heal the sick.]] In the view of the humble servant of Allah the Exalted, the benefit of this, and Allah knows best, is that the act should appear hideous to the one addressed, so that he may awaken to the fact that he ought to be averse to this vileness even where there is no legal deterrent. The reason for its hideousness is that the meaning of the verse is a rebuke to him, that his slave-girls are better than he is, because they preferred chastity to immorality, while he insists on compelling them to it. If the hidden meaning of this idea were made explicit, the deterrent would not reach the soul in its proper place. Perhaps this verse will affect base souls, so how much more the noble Arab souls. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Her saying "if" and its choice over "when" is a notification that these women used to do this willingly and voluntarily, and that what occurred from Muʿādhah and Musaykah was a rare exception. ﴿Surely Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ to them, or to them and to the women, or to both if they repent and make amends. In the recitation of Ibn ʿAbbās: "Surely Allah is Forgiving and Merciful to them." If you ask: there is no need to attach forgiveness to them, since a woman compelled to fornication is unlike the one compelled to something else in that she is not sinful. I say: perhaps the compulsion was less than what the Sharīʿah considers compulsion by killing, or by what fears destruction or loss of a limb, such as severe beating or other things, so that she is free of sin; and perhaps she fell short of the limit at which excuse is granted, so she would be sinful.

Mubayyinat: these are the verses which have made clear and explained, in this surah, the meanings of the rulings (ahkam) and the prescribed punishments (hudud). It is also possible that the original was mubayyanan fīhā (made clear within them), and the sentence was expanded by treating the place as an object (fa-ittasa'a fi al-zarf, "the adverbial phrase was extended"). It is also read with a kasra (mubayyinatin), meaning that the rulings and the prescribed punishments themselves are what have made things clear. The action is ascribed to them figuratively (ʿala al-majaz, "by way of metaphor"). Or it comes from bayyana in the sense of tabayyana (to become clear). From this is the proverb: "The dawn has become clear to the one with two eyes."

﴿And an example from those who came before you﴾: that is, a wondrous story from their stories, like the story of Yusuf and Maryam, meaning the story of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her.

﴿And an admonition﴾: what was admonished in the verses and the example, such as His saying ﴿And let not pity for them detain you in the religion of Allah﴾, and ﴿Why, when you heard it﴾, and ﴿Why, when you heard it﴾:

﴿Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of it, ever﴾.

Similar to His saying, ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾, alongside His saying, ﴿The parable of His light﴾, and ﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾:

Your saying, "Zayd is generosity and munificence," and then you say, "He uplifts people with his generosity and munificence."

The meaning is: the possessor of the light of the heavens, and the one who has the light of the heavens. The light of the heavens and the earth is the Truth. He likened it to light in its manifestness and clarity, as in His saying, ﴿Allah is the Guardian of those who believe. He brings them out of the darkness into the light﴾, i.e., from falsehood to truth.

The light is attributed to the heavens and the earth for one of two reasons. Either to indicate the breadth of its radiance and the extent of its illumination, such that the heavens and the earth are lit by it, or it is meant that the people of the heavens and the earth are those who are illuminated by it.

﴿The parable of His light﴾, i.e., the description of His light, which is wondrous in its illumination. ﴿Is like a niche (mishkah)﴾, like the description of a niche, which is an opening in a wall that does not pierce through. ﴿Within it is a lamp﴾, a large, piercing lamp, ﴿enclosed in glass﴾. He meant a lamp of Syrian glass,[[The phrase "Syrian" is an adjective modifying "glass," and it is clarified by his saying "bright." The wording of al-Nasafi is: "Shami" with a kasra on the zay, i.e., the Syrian reader recited "zujajatin" with a kasra on the zay. (ʿA)]] bright. He likened its brilliance to one of the bright stars, namely the prominent ones, such as Jupiter, Venus, Mars, Suhayl and the like. ﴿This lamp is lit from a tree﴾, i.e., its brightness began from an olive tree, meaning: its wick was soaked[[The phrase "meaning: its wick was soaked with its oil." In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): "zawaytu al-shay'" means I gathered and seized it, and "inzawat al-jildah fi al-nar" means the skin contracted and shrank in the fire. In it, "al-dhubalah" is the wick. Perhaps it is "rawaytu" with a ra, as in the wording of al-Nasafi. (ʿA)]] with its oil, ﴿blessed﴾, abundant in benefits. Or: because it grows in the land which He blessed for the worlds. It was said: seventy prophets were blessed in it, among them Ibrahim, peace be upon him. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Upon you is this tree, olive oil, so use it as a remedy, for it is a cure for hemorrhoids."[[Narrated by al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi Hatim in al-ʿIlal, Abu Nuʿaym in al-Tibb, and al-Tha'labi, all through the chain: ʿUthman ibn Salih from Ibn Lahiʿah from Yazid ibn Habib from Abu al-Khayr from ʿUtbah ibn ʿAmir, with this wording.]] ﴿Neither eastern nor western﴾, i.e., its place of growth is Syria, and the best olives are Syrian olives. It was said: it is neither in a place exposed to the sun nor in a place shaded from it,[[The phrase "wa la maqnaʾah": in al-Sihah, "al-maqʾah" is the place which the sun does not reach.]] but the sun and the shade alternate over it, and that is best for its fruit and purer for its oil. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no good in a tree in a shaded place, nor any growth in a shaded place, and there is no good in either in a sunny place."[[I have not found it.]] It was also said: it is not one upon which the sun shines only at the time of its rising or its setting, but it is struck by it in the morning and the evening alike, so it is both eastern and western. Then He described the oil with clarity and luminosity,[[The phrase "al-wabis" means gleam and shine, as stated in al-Sihah. (ʿA)]] and that, because of its brilliance, ﴿it nearly gives light even if no fire touches it﴾, ﴿light upon light﴾.

That is: this with which He likened the Truth is a multiplied light, in which the niche, the glass, the lamp and the oil have combined to assist one another, so that nothing remains of what could strengthen the light, increase its brightness, or extend its illumination, except that it is present. This is because a lamp in a confined place, such as a niche, gives more light and gathers its light better, unlike a wide place, where the light spreads out and disperses. The glass lamp is the greatest aid to increasing illumination, and likewise the oil and its purity. ﴿Allah guides to this piercing light whom He wills﴾ of His servants, i.e., He grants success in reaching the Truth through reflection and contemplation with the eye of the intellect, and through being fair to oneself, and not straying from the path that leads to it, to the right or to the left. As for one who does not reflect, he is like the blind man for whom the darkness of night and the brightness of midday are alike.

From ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth," i.e., He spread the Truth in them and disseminated it, so they were lit by its light. Or: He is the light of the hearts of their people through it. And from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with him: "The likeness of His light is the light of one who believes in Him."

It has been recited: ﴿zujājatin al-zujājah﴾, with fatḥah and kasrah. And ﴿durriyyun﴾: attributed to al-durr, i.e., white and sparkling. And ﴿durriʾun﴾, on the pattern of sakīt: it repels darkness with its light. And ﴿duriyyun﴾ like marīq. And ﴿durriyyun﴾ like al-sakīnah, reported from Abu Zayd. ﴿Tawaqqadu﴾ means ﴿tatawaqqadu﴾, and the verb refers to the glass. ﴿Yūqadu﴾ and ﴿tūqadu﴾, with lightening. ﴿Yūqadu﴾ with doubling. ﴿Yūqadu﴾ with deletion of the taʾ and fatḥah on the yāʾ, because two additional letters are gathered, and this is rare. ﴿Yamassuhu﴾ with the yāʾ, because the feminine is not real, and the pronoun is a separator.

In houses: this is connected to what precedes it, meaning "like a niche in some of the houses of Allah, which are the mosques." It is as if it were said: His light is likened to how the light of the niche appears in the mosque, whose attributes are such and such. Or it is connected to what follows, "He is glorified," meaning men glorify Him in houses. There is repetition in this, as when you say, "Zayd is in the house, sitting in it." Or it is connected to an implied verb, as in His words ﴿among nine signs﴾ (27:12), meaning "glorify [Him] in houses."

By permission (idhn) is meant command. Its being raised (rafʿ) means its being built, as in His words ﴿He raised its canopy and made it even﴾ (79:28), and ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations﴾ (2:127). From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: they are the mosques, which Allah commanded to be built. Or it means magnifying them and elevating their status. From al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: Allah did not command that they be raised by building, but by honouring them. ﴿And His name is mentioned therein﴾ (24:36) is more fitting to this, and it is general for every kind of remembrance. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: and that His Book be recited in them.

It is also read as yusabbaḥu (passive), with it attributed to one of the three adverbial phrases, namely lahu fīhā bil-ghuduww ("for Him therein in the mornings"). Men (rijāl) is in the nominative, governed by what is indicated by yusabbiḥu, which means "He is glorified for Him." It is also read tusabbiḥu, with a ta' and a kasra on the bāʾ. From Abu Jaʿfar, may Allah be pleased with him, it is read with a ta' and a fatḥa on the bāʾ. Its explanation is that it is attributed to the times of morning and evening, with the bāʾ being added, and the times are made to be the ones glorifying. The meaning is "its Lord," as in the expression "a hunt upon which are two days," meaning its wild animals (waḥsh) of both. Al-āṣāl (the evenings) is the plural of aṣīl, which is the afternoon (ʿashī).

The meaning is "at the times of the morning," that is, "at the mornings." It is also read wal-īṣāl, which is entering the late afternoon (aṣīl). It is said āṣala, like aẓhara and aʿtama.

Trade (tijāra) is the craft of the merchant, who buys and sells for profit. One possibility is that it means no kind of this craft distracts them. Then sale is specifically mentioned because it is more inclusive in distraction. A merchant who obtains a profitable sale, which is his whole aim from his craft, is distracted by it more than by anything else, namely buying something from which he expects profit at a later time, because this is certain and that is conjectural. The other possibility is that buying is called trade, applying the generic name to a species, as you say, "So-and-so's provision was a profitable trade" when a good sale or purchase came to him. It is also said that trade is for the people of importing: so-and-so traded in such-and-such when he imported it.

The tā' in iqāma (establishing) is a substitute for the middle letter that was dropped because of iʿlāl (morphological alteration). The original form was iqwām. When it became an idāfa (construct), the idāfa was placed in the position of the substitute letter, so the tā' was dropped. A similar usage is the line of poetry:

*And they broke with you the appointed time of the matter that they had promised.*

﴿And hearts and eyes will turn over﴾ (24:37) may mean either that they themselves turn over and change: they become agitated from terror and dread and fixed in a stare, as in His words ﴿when the eyes swerved and the hearts reached the throats﴾ (33:10). Or it means their states change and are altered, so that hearts come to understand after having been sealed and unable to understand, and eyes come to see after having been blind and unable to see. ﴿The best of what they did﴾ (24:38) means the best recompense for their deeds, as in His words ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward)﴾ (10:26). The meaning is that they glorify and fear, so that He rewards them with their recompense multiplied, and adds to the reward out of His bounty. Likewise the meaning of His words ﴿the best (reward) and an increase﴾ (10:26) is the good reward and an increase upon it by way of bounty. The gift of Allah the Exalted is either bounty, or reward, or compensation. ﴿And Allah gives provision to whomever He wills without reckoning﴾ (24:38): what He bestows as bounty is without reckoning, but reward has a reckoning, since it is according to what is merited.

*And they broke with you the appointed time of the matter that they had promised.*

﴿And hearts and eyes will turn over﴾ (24:37) may mean either that they themselves turn over and change: they become agitated from terror and dread and fixed in a stare, as in His words ﴿when the eyes swerved and the hearts reached the throats﴾ (33:10). Or it means their states change and are altered, so that hearts come to understand after having been sealed and unable to understand, and eyes come to see after having been blind and unable to see. ﴿The best of what they did﴾ (24:38) means the best recompense for their deeds, as in His words ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward)﴾ (10:26). The meaning is that they glorify and fear, so that He rewards them with their recompense multiplied, and adds to the reward out of His bounty. Likewise the meaning of His words ﴿the best (reward) and an increase﴾ (10:26) is the good reward and an increase upon it by way of bounty. The gift of Allah the Exalted is either bounty, or reward, or compensation. ﴿And Allah gives provision to whomever He wills without reckoning﴾ (24:38): what He bestows as bounty is without reckoning, but reward has a reckoning, since it is according to what is merited.

In houses: this is connected to what precedes it, meaning "like a niche in some of the houses of Allah, which are the mosques." It is as if it were said: His light is likened to how the light of the niche appears in the mosque, whose attributes are such and such. Or it is connected to what follows, "He is glorified," meaning men glorify Him in houses. There is repetition in this, as when you say, "Zayd is in the house, sitting in it." Or it is connected to an implied verb, as in His words ﴿among nine signs﴾ (27:12), meaning "glorify [Him] in houses."

By permission (idhn) is meant command. Its being raised (rafʿ) means its being built, as in His words ﴿He raised its canopy and made it even﴾ (79:28), and ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations﴾ (2:127). From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: they are the mosques, which Allah commanded to be built. Or it means magnifying them and elevating their status. From al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: Allah did not command that they be raised by building, but by honouring them. ﴿And His name is mentioned therein﴾ (24:36) is more fitting to this, and it is general for every kind of remembrance. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: and that His Book be recited in them.

It is also read as yusabbaḥu (passive), with it attributed to one of the three adverbial phrases, namely lahu fīhā bil-ghuduww ("for Him therein in the mornings"). Men (rijāl) is in the nominative, governed by what is indicated by yusabbiḥu, which means "He is glorified for Him." It is also read tusabbiḥu, with a ta' and a kasra on the bāʾ. From Abu Jaʿfar, may Allah be pleased with him, it is read with a ta' and a fatḥa on the bāʾ. Its explanation is that it is attributed to the times of morning and evening, with the bāʾ being added, and the times are made to be the ones glorifying. The meaning is "its Lord," as in the expression "a hunt upon which are two days," meaning its wild animals (waḥsh) of both. Al-āṣāl (the evenings) is the plural of aṣīl, which is the afternoon (ʿashī).

The meaning is "at the times of the morning," that is, "at the mornings." It is also read wal-īṣāl, which is entering the late afternoon (aṣīl). It is said āṣala, like aẓhara and aʿtama.

Trade (tijāra) is the craft of the merchant, who buys and sells for profit. One possibility is that it means no kind of this craft distracts them. Then sale is specifically mentioned because it is more inclusive in distraction. A merchant who obtains a profitable sale, which is his whole aim from his craft, is distracted by it more than by anything else, namely buying something from which he expects profit at a later time, because this is certain and that is conjectural. The other possibility is that buying is called trade, applying the generic name to a species, as you say, "So-and-so's provision was a profitable trade" when a good sale or purchase came to him. It is also said that trade is for the people of importing: so-and-so traded in such-and-such when he imported it.

**Al-Sarab** is what appears in the desert at midday of sunlight, which flows over the surface of the earth as though it were running water. **Al-qay'a** means *al-qa'* (the flat, level ground), or is the plural of *qa'*, the level and even expanse of land, like *jayra* as the plural of *jar*. It has been read as **bi-qay'at**, with the taa' written as an elongated taa' (*ta' mamtuda*), like *dimat* and *qaymat* as the plurals of *dima* and *qayma*. Some have read it as **bi-qay'a'**, with a round taa' (*ta' marbuta*), like *rajul 'azhaha* (a man who is very averse to speech and effort). The verse likens the deeds of one who does not hold faith and does not follow the truth, deeds of righteousness which he supposes will benefit him with God and save him from His punishment, but which in the end disappoint his hope and meet with the opposite of what he had planned, to a mirage that the disbeliever sees in the desert plain (*al-sahira*). On the Day of Resurrection, thirst overcomes him, so he supposes it to be water, and he comes to it but finds nothing of what he hoped for. There he finds God's angels of punishment (*zabaniya*) seizing him, dragging him by the neck to Hell, and giving him to drink from the boiling water (*hamim*) and the dreadful pus (*ghassaq*). These are the ones of whom God said: ﴿Toiling and weary﴾, ﴿and they think that they are doing good work﴾, ﴿And We will turn to the deeds they did and make them scattered dust﴾.

It has also been said: the verse was revealed concerning ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa ibn Umayya, who had been devout in the time of ignorance (*jahiliyya*), wore sackcloth, and sought religion, but then disbelieved after Islam.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 24, verse 40:

Al-lujji: the deep, abundant in water, derived from al-lujj, which is the greater part of the sea's water. In "akhraja" (he brought out), the pronoun refers to the one who is in it. "Lam yakad yarahā" (he almost did not see it) is an intensification of "lam yarahā" (he did not see it), meaning: he did not come close to seeing it, let alone actually seeing it. A similar line is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"When distance alters the lovers, the lingering trace of passion does not depart from love of Mayya.
Neither does nearness approach her out of weariness, nor does her love dwindle when the home is far away."

This is by Dhu al-Rummah. Al-nay' means distance. It is said "rassa" and "arassa" when something persists. Al-rasis is the remnant of illness that stays lodged within the body.

"Yabrah" means "yadhhab" (goes away); that is, he did not come close to al-biraḥ (the open space), so how could it go away? It is related that when Dhu al-Rummah came to Kufa, Ibn Shubrumah objected to him about this, saying that it indicates the disappearance of the lingering trace of passion. So Dhu al-Rummah changed it to his saying: "lam ajid" (I did not find). Ibn 'Utbah said: I told my father about this, and he said:

"Ibn Shubrumah was wrong, and Dhu al-Rummah was wrong in changing it; rather, it is like the saying of God, Exalted: lam yakad yarahā."

"Al-mallah" means weariness. "Tanzah" means "tub'ad" (goes far). "Yanzah" means "yazul" (departs).

That is: he did not come close to al-biraḥ (the open space), so why would it depart? He compared their deeds, first, in the loss of their benefit and the presence of their harm, to a mirage which the one deceived by it does not find anything of from afar, and his disappointment and grief were not enough for him, as he did not find anything like others who found mirage, until he found with it the guardians of Hell dragging him to the Fire, and it does not quench his thirst with water. And he compared them, second, in their darkness and blackness because they are false, and in their emptiness of the light of truth, to layers of darkness from the depths of the sea, the waves and the clouds. Then he said: "And whoever God does not grant the light of His guidance, His protection and His kindness, then he has no light, being in the darkness of falsehood."

This discourse is of the nature of metaphors (kinayat), because the subtle favours of God only follow faith and deed, or are awaited for them. Do you not see His saying: "And those who strive in Us, We shall surely guide them to Our paths" (29:69), and His saying: "And God leads the wrongdoers astray" (14:27)?

It is also read: "saḥābun ẓulumātun" (clouds of darkness), in the idafa construction. And "saḥābun ẓulumātun," with "saḥābun" in the nominative and nunated, and "ka-ẓulumātin" in the genitive, as a substitute (badal) for the first "ẓulumātun."

Ṣāffāt: spreading and arranging their wings in the air. The pronoun in ʿalima (ʿalima, "He knows") refers either to each (of them) or to God. Likewise in ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu (ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu, "their prayer and their glorification"), and ṣalāh (ṣalāh, "prayer") here means supplication (duʿāʾ). It is not far-fetched that God should inspire the birds with their supplication and glorification, just as He inspired them with the other subtle sciences which intelligent beings can scarcely come to know.
