Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 24, verses 43–44:

**يُزْجِي** means *yasuqu* (drives along). From it comes **al-bidaa'a al-muzjaah** (the meager merchandise), which is the goods that everyone offers but no one is content with.

The cloud (**al-sahab**) is used as a singular, like *al-‘amaa’*, and as a collective, like *al-rabaab*. [[His saying "like al-rabaab": in al-Sihah, al-Rabaab, with a fatha on the ra', is a white cloud. (A)]] The meaning of the singular being formed into a whole is that it becomes scattered fragments (**qaza'**), and some of it is joined to other parts. The word **bayn** (between) was permitted with it although it is singular, because the meaning lies between its parts, as was said in the line:

*"... bayn al-dukhul fa-hawmal"* [[*Qifa nabki min dhikra habibin wa manzili... bi-saqti al-liwa bayna al-dukhuli fa-hawmali.* This is the opening line of the mu'allaqa of Imru' al-Qays. It is reported that he reached adolescence without having composed poetry, so his father said, "He is not a man of worth." He ordered two of his close attendants to take him to a distant place and slaughter him there. When they were about to slaughter him, he wept and recited the verse through to the end of the qasida, so they brought him back. They said: "This is the best poet on the face of the earth. He stood and made others stand, wept and made others weep, remembered and made others remember, and the beloved and the dwelling are in half a line." **Al-saqt** (with three vowel options) is the edge of the **liwa**, meaning the winding, crooked place. Here it is the proper name of a specific place. **Bayn** is not prefixed except to something plural in meaning, or to something coordinated with it by waw alone. So the meaning is "between the parts of al-Dukhul and Hawmal," that is, both are place names, and perhaps the "saqt al-liwa" extends between them. It is also possible that the fa' (in fa-hawmal) means waw, so that "saqt al-liwa" lies between these two places, and the use of fa' here indicates how close al-Dukhul and Hawmal are to one another.]]

**Al-rukaam** is that which is piled up, one part upon another. **Al-wadq** is the rain. **Min khilalihi** means from its openings and outlets; it is the plural of *khalal*, like *jibaal* for *jabal*. It was also read as *min khallihi*. **Wa yunazzilu** is read with the doubled letter. **Yakaadu sanaa** is read with assimilation [[His saying "yakaadu sanaa with assimilation": perhaps its orthography was *yakaasanaa*, unless one considers what came before the assimilation. (A)]].

**Barquhu** is the plural of **barqah**, which means a measure of lightning, like *ghurfa* (a handful) and *luqma* (a mouthful). **Barquhu** is also read with two damma vowels for the sake of harmony, as was said of the plural of *fi'la* being *fi'alaat*, like *zulumaat*. **Sanaa'a barquhu** with a short alif is in the sense of light (**al-dau'**). With a long alif (**al-mamduud**) it means height and elevation, from your saying *sanii*, meaning elevated.

**Yadhhabu bil-absaar** is read with the extra **ba'** as in His saying *wa laa tulquu bi-aydikum* (and do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction). This is related from Abu Ja'far al-Madani.

This is part of enumerating the proofs of His lordship and the manifestation of His command, for He mentioned the glorification of all who are in the heavens and the earth, and all that flies between heaven and earth, and their supplication and their entreaty to Him. He made the clouds subject in the manner that was described, and what happens within them by His acts, until the rain comes down from them. He distributes His mercy among His creatures, withholds it and extends it according to what His wisdom requires. He shows them the lightning in the cloud that nearly snatches away their sight, so that they may take heed and be wary. He alternates night and day and makes them differ in length and shortness. These are nothing but proofs of the utmost clarity of His existence and permanence, and signs that proclaim His attributes to whoever looks, reflects, perceives and contemplates.

If you say: when did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) see the glorification and supplication of those in the heavens, and the glorification and supplication of the birds, and the sending down of rain from mountains of hail in the sky, such that it was said to him, "Did you not see?" I say: he knew it through God's informing him of it by way of revelation.

If you say: what is the difference between the first, second and third *min* in His saying *min al-sama'i min jibaalin, min barad*?

I say: the first is for the starting point (ibtida' al-ghaya), the second is for partitioning (tab'id), and the third is for explanation (bayan). Or the first two are for the starting point, and the last for partitioning. The meaning is that He sends down hail from the sky, from mountains in it. On the first reading, the object of *yunazzilu* is *min jibaalin*.

If you say: what is the meaning of *min jibaalin fiiha min barad*? I say: it has two meanings. One is that God creates mountains of hail in the sky, just as He created mountains of stone on the earth. The second is that by mentioning mountains He intends abundance, as one says, "So-and-so owns mountains of gold."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 24, verse 45:

It is also recited: "khāliqu kulli dābbah" (the Creator of every moving creature). Since the term dābbah (moving creature) applies both to those that discern and to those that do not, the discerning ones predominate, and what lies beyond them is given their ruling, as though all moving creatures were discerning. For this reason it is said: "fa-minhum" (among them, in the masculine plural form for rational beings), and it is said: "man yamshī ʿalā baṭn" (of them is that which walks on its belly) and "wa-l-māshī ʿalā arbaʿ qawāʾim" (and that which walks on four legs). If you ask: why is "māʾ" (water) indefinite in His words "min māʾin" (from water)?

I say: because the meaning is that He created every moving creature from a kind of water specific to that creature; or He created them from a specific water, which is the sperm-drop (nuṭfah), and then He varied the created beings in respect of the sperm-drop, so that among them are insects, among them are beasts, and among them are humans.

Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: "yusqā bi-māʾin wāḥidin wa-nufaḍḍilu baʿḍahā ʿalā baʿḍin fī l-ukul" (They are watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit) [Q. 13:4]. If you ask: then why is it definite in His words "wa-jaʿalnā min al-māʾi kulla shayʾin ḥayy" (And We made from water every living thing) [Q. 21:30]? I say: there He intends another meaning, namely that all kinds of animals are created from this kind [[Maḥmūd said: "If you ask why māʾ is indefinite here but definite in His words 'wa-jaʿalnā min al-māʾi kulla shayʾin ḥayy'? I say: the purpose in our present verse is that He, exalted is He, created every moving creature from a kind of water specific to it, namely the sperm-drop, and then varied the created beings according to the variation of their drops, so that some are thus and some are thus. Similar to it is His saying 'yusqā bi-māʾin wāḥidin wa-nufaḍḍilu baʿḍahā ʿalā baʿḍin fī l-ukul'. As for the verse 'iqtarab' (Q. 21:30 is the verse intended), its purpose is that all kinds of animals are created from this kind." Aḥmad said: The distinction in detail is that the aim in the first is to show the sign that from one thing, by power, diverse things came into being, the details of which are mentioned in the verses of al-Nūr and al-Raʿd. The aim in the verse "iqtarab" is that He created things agreed in the genus of life from the genus of water, which has differing types; so it is mentioned in the definite form to include its differing types. Thus the verse in the first case is for bringing out the diverse from the uniform. And God knows best.]] which is the genus of water, because it is the origin, even though intermediaries intervene between it and them. They said: He created the angels from light, which He created from water; the jinn from fire, which He created from it; and Adam from earth, which He created from it. If you ask: why have the three genera come in this order? I say:

He placed first what is more eminent in power, namely that which moves without an instrument of motion, from feet or legs; then that which walks on two legs; then that which walks on four. If you ask: why is crawling on the belly called "walking" (mashy)? I say: it is by way of metaphor, as they say of a continuing matter: "this matter has walked (qad mashā hādhā l-amr)," and it is said: "so-and-so's affair does not walk for him (lā yatamashsha lahu amr)."

Similar to this is the metaphorical use of "shafah" (lip) in place of "juḥfalah" (the upper lip of a solid-hoofed animal), and "mishfar" (thick lip) in place of "shafah" (lip), and the like. Or it is by way of harmonizing with the mention of the crawler alongside the walkers.

وَمَا أُولَئِكَ بِالْمُؤْمِنِينَ: This refers to those who said "We believe and we obey." Or it refers to the faction that turned away. The meaning on the first view is an announcement from God that faith is negated from all of them, not only from the faction that turned away. On the second view:

It is an announcement that the faction that turned away never had true faith in what had preceded from them; rather, it was a claim made with the tongue without the agreement of the heart, because if it had come from a sound belief and a settled soul, it would not have been followed by turning away and aversion.

The definite article in His words "بِالْمُؤْمِنِينَ" (the believers) indicates that they are not the believers you know of: those who are steadfast and upright in faith, described in His words, exalted is He, "إِنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا بِاللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَرْتَابُوا" ("The believers are only those who have believed in God and His Messenger and then did not doubt").

Al-Hasan said: "The saying of the believers" (qawl al-mu'minin), with the nominative and the accusative, is stronger, because the more definite of the two nouns is the one that should be the subject of kāna (the verb "to be" in its role as a copular verb), and that is "qawl" in the phrase "qawl al-mu'minin"... Let me correct that and give the passage exactly as it stands:

And on the authority of al-Hasan: "qawl al-mu'minin" (the saying of the believers), with the nominative and the accusative, is stronger, because the more definite of the two nouns is the one that should be the subject of kāna (the copular verb "to be"), being the more definite of the two: and that they should say "awghal" (the more definite form), since there is no way to make it indefinite, unlike "qawl al-mu'minin." Recited variants: "wa-yattaqhi" (with the qaf and ha vowelled with kasra, both with and without pause), and also with the ha sukun; and with the qaf sukun and ha kasra, the form being likened to "katf" (shoulder) and lightened, as in the verse of the poet:

قالت سليمى اشتر لنا سويقا ... وهات خبز البرّ أو دقيقا

(Qalat Sulayma: ishtur lana suwayqan... wa-hat khubz al-barr aw daqiqan)

It is by al-Adhafir al-Kindi. It is said: "shara al-'asal" and "ishtarahu" (to honey and the like), meaning: when one gathers it and takes it from its place. So his saying "ishtur" is an imperative from al-ishtiyar. It may also be from al-ishtira' (buying), and its ra' was made sukun out of necessity, meaning: seek for us suwayq. Suwayq is what the Arabs make from wheat and barley. "Hat" (bring): with a kasra on the ta', an imperative for the masculine; she asked him for suwayq as a relish, and gave him the choice between bringing bread or bringing flour, for she would bake it. It is also narrated: "wa-hat bur al-bakhs aw daqiqan", and al-bakhs is land that grows without irrigation. In the rest of the rajaz she asked him for meat, a servant, and dye for her clothes with safflower, so he said:

يا سلم لو كنت لذا مطيقا ... ما كان عيشى عندكم ترنيقا

(Ya Salm, law kunta li-dha mutiqan... ma kana 'aysi 'indakum tarniqan)

That is, the duration of the bird's tarnīq, i.e., its spreading of its wings in the air.

Allah has gathered in this verse the causes of success. Ibn 'Abbas, in its interpretation, said: "Whoever obeys Allah" in His obligations, "and His Messenger" in his sunan, "and fears Allah" concerning what has passed of his sins, "and fears Him" concerning what is yet to come.

It is also narrated that one of the kings asked about a comprehensive verse, and this verse was recited to him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 24, verse 53:

"Jahd aymanihi" (their most earnest oaths): a metaphor taken from "jahd nafsihi" (the utmost of one's capacity), when one reaches the limit of one's capacity. This is when one swears emphatically and reaches the utmost of its intensity and vehemence. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever says 'by Allah', [he has] jahd yamīnihi." The original form is: "aqsama jahd al-yamīn" (he swore the utmost of oaths), meaning: "aqsama yajhadu al-yamīna jahdan" (he swore, exerting the utmost in the oath). The verb was deleted and the verbal noun (maṣdar) was placed first, so it was put in its position in the form of an annexed noun (muḍāf) to its object, as in the words: "faḍraba al-riqāb" (striking the necks). The rule for this accusative noun is the rule of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if he had said: "jāhidīna aymānahum" (exerting their oaths).

"Ṭāʿatun maʿrūfatun" (an obedience known): it is the predicate of a deleted subject (khabar mubtadaʾ maḥdhūf), or a subject with a deleted predicate, meaning: your command, or what is sought from you, is a known, recognized obedience about which there is no doubt or suspicion, like the obedience of the sincere believers whose inner state matches their outer state, not oaths that you swear with your mouths while your hearts contradict them. Or your obedience is a known obedience, in that it is by speech only, not by deed. Or a known obedience is more fitting and better for you than these lying oaths.

Al-Yazidi read it as "ṭāʿatan maʿrūfatan" (in the accusative), meaning: "obey with a known obedience."

"Inna Allaha khabīrun" (Indeed Allah is All-Aware): He knows what is in your inner selves, nothing of your secrets is hidden from Him, and He will surely expose you and requite you for your hypocrisy.

Zamakhshari's commentary on Surah al-Nur, verse 54 (al-Kashshaf):

He turned the speech away from the third person (absence) to the second person (address), by way of iltifat (shifting of pronouns), and this is more forceful in rebuking them. The meaning is:

"But if you turn away, then he has not harmed Him at all; rather, you have harmed yourselves. The Messenger is only responsible for what Allah has laden him with and charged him with, namely conveying the message. When he has conveyed it, he has discharged his obligation. As for you, what is incumbent upon you is what you were charged with: receiving it with acceptance and submission. If you do not do so and turn away, you have exposed yourselves to the wrath and punishment of Allah. But if you obey him, you have secured your share of coming out of misguidance into guidance. Thus benefit and harm return to you. The Messenger is only a sincere advisor and guide, and his only duty is to convey what benefits you if you accept it [[the phrase "in your acceptance": the wording of al-Nasafi is "in your hearts": (ʿ)]], and there is no harm to him in your turning away."

Al-balagh (the conveying) means al-tabligh (the act of conveying), like al-ada' (the discharge) means al-ta'diyah (the act of discharging). The meaning of al-mubin (the clear) is that it is accompanied by the signs (ayat) and miracles (mu'jizat).

The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and to those with him. *Minkum* ("from among you") is explanatory (*li-l-bayan*), as in the one at the end of Surah al-Fath: God promised them that He would give Islam victory over disbelief, make them inheritors of the land and appoint them as successors (*khulafa'*) in it, as He did with the Children of Israel when He made them inheritors of Egypt and the Levant after destroying the tyrants, and that He would establish the religion He has approved, which is the religion of Islam. *Tamkin* (establishment) means making it firm and secure. He would also make their state secure and remove the fear they had been in. The Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions had stayed in Mecca for ten years in fear. When they emigrated, they were in Medina, where they would rise and retire in arms. A man said: "Will there be no day when we are safe and can put down our weapons?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You will not remain (in this state) except briefly, until one of you sits in a great assembly, cross-legged (*muhtabiyan*), without any iron weapon with him." [Footnote: The phrase "*la tughayyiruna illa yasiran*" in the text is explained as meaning "you will not remain (so) except a little," as stated in al-Sihah (the lexicon). (Ea.)]

[Footnote: al-Tabari narrated it through Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding God's words ﴿God has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the land﴾. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) remained for ten years in fear, calling to God secretly and openly. Then he was commanded to emigrate to Medina, and he and his companions remained there... (to the end). al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it with its beginning omitted, with the mention of Ubayy ibn Ka'b in it. Its beginning is: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions arrived in Medina and the Ansar sheltered them, the Arabs shot at them from one bow. They did not spend the night except armed... (the hadith)."]

God fulfilled His promise, gave them dominion over the Arabian Peninsula, and afterwards they conquered the lands of the East and the West, tore apart the kingdom of the Persian emperors (*al-akasira*), took possession of their treasuries, and seized control of the world. Then those who departed from their way came out, and they disbelieved in those blessings and transgressed. This is the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The caliphate after me will last thirty years; then God will give kingship to whomever He wills, and it will become a kingdom; then it will become *bazizi*:"

[Footnote: On his words "*tasir bazizi*": in al-Sihah, *bazzahu yabuzzuhu bazzan* means he stripped him (plundered him). The noun *al-bazizi* is like *al-khusaysi*. (Ea.)]

"Highway robbery, shedding of blood, and taking of wealth without right."

[Footnote: I have not found it. Its beginning in al-Sunan (of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi), Ibn Majah, al-Hakim, Ahmad, al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi and al-Tha'labi, all from the hadith of Safinah, is: "The caliphate in my community is thirty years, then kingship after kingship," and in another wording: "then God gives kingship to whomever He wills." Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tabarani narrated through 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, from Abu Tha'labah, from Abu 'Ubaydah and Mu'adh ibn Jabal, with a raised (*marfu'*) chain: "God began this matter as prophethood, then it will become a caliphate... (the hadith)."]

It is recited as *kama istakhlafa* (with the verb in the passive, "as those before them were made successors"). And *wa-li-yubaddilannahum* is read with the doubled letter (*bi-l-tashdid*).

If you ask: where is the oath marked by the *lam* and the *nun* in *la-yastakhlifannahum*? I answer: it is omitted, its implied sense being: "God promised them, and swore that He would surely make them successors." Or, the promise of God was treated, in its certainty, as having the status of an oath, so it takes what an oath takes, as if it were said: "God swore that He would surely make them successors."

If you ask: what is the position (*mahall*) of *ya'buduna-ni* (they worship Me)? I answer: if you take it as a resumptive clause (*istinaf*), it has no position in the sentence, as if someone asked: "Why do they become successors and feel secure?" And the answer is: "They worship Me." If you take it as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to *wa'adahum* (He promised them), meaning God promised them this while they were worshipping and sincere, then its position is in the accusative (*nasb*).

*Wa-man kafara* ("and whoever disbelieves") means ingratitude for blessings, like His words ﴿so she disbelieved in the blessings of God﴾. *Fa-ulaika hum al-fasiqun* ("those are the transgressors") means: they are the complete ones in their transgression, since they disbelieved that great blessing and dared to scorn it.

[Footnote: On his words "*ghamtiha*": meaning belittling it, holding it in contempt. (Ea.)]

If you ask: does this verse contain evidence for the caliphate of the Rightly Guided Caliphs? I answer: it is the clearest and most manifest evidence, because the successors who believed and did righteous deeds are precisely those (the Rightly Guided Caliphs).

"And establish the prayer" is coordinated with "obey Allah and obey the Messenger." It is not far-fetched that a separating element should fall between the conjoined element and that to which it is conjoined, even if it is long, since the proper character of the conjoined element is that it be other than the element it is conjoined to. The obedience to the Messenger was repeated for emphasis on its being obligatory.

Also read: lā yaḥsabanna (with the yā’, "let them not think"). In this reading there are several possibilities. One is that muʿjizīna fī al-arḍ (“outpacing [Allah] on earth”) are the two objects.

The meaning is: let not those who disbelieve think that anyone can outpace Allah on earth, so that they [themselves] hope for the like of that. This is a strong and sound meaning.

Another possibility is that the pronoun in it refers to the Messenger, since he was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿And obey the Messenger﴾. A further possibility is that the original form was: lā yaḥsabannahum alladhīna kafarū muʿjizīn ("let not those who disbelieve think them outpacing [Allah]"), and then the pronoun that is the first object was deleted. What permitted this is that when the subject and the two objects refer to one and the same thing, it suffices to mention two of them instead of the third. He also linked His saying, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾, to lā yaḥsabanna alladhīna kafarū muʿjizīn, as if it were said: "Those who disbelieve will not escape Allah, and their refuge is the Fire." What is meant by them is those who swear their oaths with utmost effort.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 24, verse 58:

He commanded that the slaves seek permission. It has also been said: the slaves, the female slaves, and the children who have not reached puberty, from among the free, must seek permission three times in the day and night: before the Dawn Prayer (ṣalāt al-fajr), because it is the time of rising from the beds, discarding the clothes one sleeps in, and putting on the clothes of wakefulness; at midday (ẓahīra), because it is the time of removing clothes for the qā'ila (the midday rest); and after the Night Prayer (ṣalāt al-'ishā'), because it is the time of stripping off the clothes of wakefulness and wrapping oneself in the clothes of sleep. Each of these states is called ʿawra, because people's covering and guarding of themselves is disturbed in them. And ʿawra means a flaw. From it comes:

"a'war al-fāris" [[His comment on "and from it: a'war al-fāris" – in the Ṣiḥāḥ, a'war al-fāris means that a place of flaw has appeared in him for a blow. (ʿ: the editor)]] (the horseman became exposed, i.e. a vulnerable spot appeared in him), and "a'war al-makān" (the place became exposed), and al-a'war (one whose eye is defective). Then He excused them from seeking permission beyond these times, and explained the reason for the excuse in His words: ﴿They go round about you, some of you to others﴾, meaning: there is a need on your part and theirs for mixing and frequenting: they go round about you for service, and you go round about them for employment. So if the command to seek permission were made absolute at every time, it would lead to hardship. It is reported that Mudlij ibn ʿAmr, who was a young Ansari boy, was sent by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at midday to ʿUmar to summon him. He entered upon him while he was sleeping and his garment had come uncovered from him. ʿUmar said: "I wish that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had forbidden our fathers, our sons and our servants from entering upon us at these times except with permission." Then he set out with him to the Prophet ﷺ, and found that this verse had been revealed to him [[Thus al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) reported it without a chain of narration.]]: and it is one of the verses revealed on account of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him). It has also been said: it was revealed concerning Asmāʾ bint Abī Murthid [[His comment "and it has been said it was revealed concerning Asmāʾ bint Abī Murthid" – perhaps it is Murthid, as in the wording of al-Nasafi. (ʿ: the editor)]], who said: "We enter upon a man and a woman, and perhaps they are under one blanket" [[Thus al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi reported it from Muqatil.]].

It has also been said: a large boy of hers entered upon her at a time she disliked his entering, so she came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "Our servants and our boys enter upon us in a state we dislike." It is reported from Abū ʿAmr: al-ḥulum (puberty) with a sukūn (vowel-less letter).

It was also read ﴿thalāthu ʿawrātin﴾ in the accusative as a substitute for "thalāth marrāt," meaning: the times of three ʿawrāt. And from al-Aʿmash: ʿawrāt in the dialect of Hudhayl. If you ask: what is the position of "laysa ʿalaykum" (there is no blame upon you)? I say: if "thalāthu ʿawrātin" is put in the nominative, it is in the position of the nominative as a qualifier, and the meaning is: they are three ʿawrāt specified for seeking permission. If it is put in the accusative, it has no position, and it is a statement affirming the command to seek permission in those specific states. If you ask: by what is "baʿḍukum" in the nominative? I say: it is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ʿalā baʿḍin, in the sense of "going round about some upon others," and it is omitted because "ṭawwāfūna" indicates it. It is also permissible that it be in the nominative governed by a hidden "yaṭūfu," for that same indication.

The children among you: meaning free children, not the slaves (al-mamalik), who are among those before them. He means: those who have reached puberty (al-hulm) from among them, who are the men. Or: those mentioned before them in His words, ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants﴾, to the end of the verse. The meaning is that children are permitted to enter without permission except at the three times of privacy (al-'awrat al-thalath). When children have become accustomed to this and then pass the limit of childhood, by having a wet dream or reaching the age at which they are judged to be adults, they must be weaned from that habit and required to ask permission at all times, like the grown men who were not accustomed to entering upon you except with permission. People are heedless of this matter, and to them it is like an abrogated law (shari'a mansukha). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "The verse that most people do not believe in is the verse of permission. I instruct my neighbour's women to ask permission to enter upon me." 'Ata' was asked: "Should I ask permission to enter upon my sister?" He said: "Yes, even if she is in your care and you support her," and he recited this verse. It is also related from him: "There are three verses that people have denied: the verse on permission in its entirety; the words ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you﴾, where some people said, 'the most important of you is the one with the largest house'; and the words ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives﴾." It is related from Ibn Mas'ud: "You must ask permission to enter upon your fathers, mothers and sisters." It is related from al-Sha'bi that it is not abrogated. It was said to him, "People do not act upon it," and he said, "God is the one whose help is sought." It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "They say it is abrogated, but by God, it is not abrogated; rather, people have been negligent about it."

If you ask, what is the age at which one is judged to have reached puberty? I say: Abu Hanifa said eighteen years for a boy and seventeen for a girl. The majority of scholars say fifteen for both. It is related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that he used to judge by height and estimate it at five spans (ashbar). The poet al-Farazdaq followed this in his words:

He has not ceased since his hands fastened his waistcloth,
and he rose and reached the height of five spans.

He brings close the swaying (banners) of one to another that meet
in the shade of a dust-cloud raised fresh and stirred up.

These lines are by al-Farazdaq, in an elegy for Yazid ibn al-Muhallab. He says: he has not ceased to fight since the time his hands fastened his waistcloth, which is a metaphor for his attaining discernment and taking charge of his own affairs. "Mudh" is a temporal adverb, since it is followed by a clause, but it also conveys the sense of a starting point, because the meaning is: he has not ceased to plunge into wars from the time he reached maturity until he died. Attributing the fastening to the hands is a figurative attribution to the instrument, since he fastened with them. "Sama" means he rose, so that his stature reached the measure of five spans. It is said that this refers to the length of a sword, a metaphor for his reaching maturity. It is also said that it refers to the length of a grave, and "reaching it" is a metaphor for his death. That is: from the time of his discernment until the time of his death he stirred up wars, and this is more eloquent in meaning. The conjunction "then (fa)" with "adraka" indicates the shortness of his life span and the nearness of his death. It is also narrated as "fa-sama" with fa.

It may also mean: his rank rose, so that it covers all his states. His words "yudni" are the predicate of "ma zal", meaning: he brings close restless banners to others, or restless horses to similar ones in battle. The meaning is that he brings the battalions close to one another until they all meet in the shade of a fresh dust-cloud. "Mu'tabat" with the unpointed 'ayn is a passive participle, meaning that no one had fought in it before him, so that he stirred it up from its place; rather, he was the one who raised it. Or it means he was the one who brought it out from the hard ground, so that it did not exist before. It is also narrated with the dotted ghayn, "mughtabat", meaning abundant: the meaning is that it was increased and multiplied by him. It may also be a place name. It is also narrated as "mu'tarak al-'ajaj", which is the place of battle; "al-'ajaj" is dust. "Mathar" is an adjective of "mu'tabat" if it is not made definite by an annexed noun. It is possible that its original form was "mathariuhu", with an annexed pronoun, which was omitted for metrical necessity. The attribution of shade to the fresh, stirred-up dust indicates that it was dense, blocking the sunlight from the fighters. Others took "al-inbat" (growth of hair) as the sign of puberty. It is related from 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, that he was asked about a boy, and he said: "Has his waistcloth turned green?"

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 24, verse 60:

al-qā'id (al-qawā'id): those women who have ceased menstruating and bearing children because of their age. lā yarjūna nikāḥan: who do not hope for marriage, do not desire it. The meaning of "garments" here is the outer garments, such as the milhafa (wrap) and the jilbab, which is worn over the khimar (head-covering). ghayra mutabarrijātin bi-zīnatin: not displaying adornment, not showing their finery.

[[Ahmad said: al-Zamakhshari established this verse upon its apparent meaning. It appears to me, and God knows best, that His saying ﴿not displaying adornment﴾ is of the type of the line:

"On a smooth road whose landmark one cannot be guided by,"

meaning: there is no landmark in it by which one could be guided. Likewise, the intended meaning here is: "and the women past childbearing who have no adornment with which they would display themselves," because the discussion concerns those in this condition. It seems that the purpose is that for these women, abstaining from removing their garments is better for them, so consider what of women who possess adornment in garments. The most eloquent point in this is that He made the non-removal of garments, with regard to elderly women, a matter of chastity, signaling that the removal of garments has no bearing on chastity. This is said regarding elderly women; how much more so regarding young women? And God knows best.]]

It means the light adornment that He intended in His saying ﴿and not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾, or [those who are] not intending by removing their garments a display (tabarruj), but when they need to lighten their dress, [it is permitted]. Abstaining from removing it is better for them. Since he mentioned the permissible, he followed it with the recommended, seeking the choice of the best and finest deeds, as in His saying ﴿and that you pardon is nearer to righteousness﴾, and ﴿and that you give charity is better for you﴾.

If you say: what is the reality of tabarruj? I say: it is the affectation of displaying what must be concealed, from the expression "a ship barij," meaning one with no covering over it. And al-baraj is the width of the eye, in which its whiteness surrounds its blackness entirely, with nothing of it hidden; except that it is specifically used for a woman unveiling herself to men by showing her adornment and displaying her charms. And "badā" and "baraza," meaning "appeared," are among the cognates of tabarruj and taballuj, likewise.

The believers used to take the weak and the disabled to the houses of their spouses and children, and to the houses of their relatives and friends, and they would feed them from those houses. So doubt arose in the hearts of both those who fed and those who were fed, and they feared that some blame might fall on them for this, and they disliked that it should be eating without right, because of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾. So it was said to them: there is no blame upon the weak, nor upon yourselves; meaning, there is no blame upon you, nor upon those believers who are in a situation like yours, in this matter. It is related from ʿIkrimah: the Ansar had a scruple within themselves [[The phrase "in their selves there was a qazzaza": in al-Sihah, "al-qazzaza" means fastidiousness and keeping far from defilement. And in it "al-tanass" means excessive purification. (ʿA)]], so they would not eat from these houses when they were well-off. It was also said: these people would avoid sitting with people and eating with them, lest something should lead to aversion on their part; and because the blind man's hand may reach what his dining companion's eye has reached without his noticing; and the lame man spreads out in his seat and takes more than his place, crowding his companion; and the sick man is not free of an offensive smell, or a wound that oozes, or a nose that runs, and the like. It was also said: they used to go out to raid and leave the weak behind in their houses, handing them the keys and permitting them to eat from their houses, but they would feel scrupulous about it. It is related from al-Harith ibn ʿAmr that he went out raiding and left Malik ibn Zayd in his house and his property; when he returned he saw him in a state of want, and said: What has befallen you? He said: I had nothing, and it was not lawful for me to eat from your property. So it was said: there is no blame upon these weak people for what they were scrupulous about, nor is there blame upon you for eating from these houses. This is a correct statement. Likewise, if it is interpreted as: there is no blame upon these people for remaining behind from the raid, and no blame upon you for eating from the aforementioned houses, because the two groups share in that each of them is free of blame. An example of this: a traveler asks you about breaking the fast in Ramadan, and a pilgrim in ihram asks about putting the shaving before the sacrifice; you say: there is no blame upon the traveler for breaking his fast, and no blame upon you, O pilgrim, for putting the shaving before the sacrifice. If you say: why was the children not mentioned? I say: their mention is included under His saying ﴿from your houses﴾, because a man's child is part of him, and his ruling is the ruling of himself. And in the hadith: "The best that a man eats is from his earnings, and his child is from his earnings" [[Related by the authors of the Sunan, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Bazzar and Abu Yaʿla, all from the hadith of ʿAʾishah in this wording. Ibn al-Qattan said: ʿUmarah ibn ʿUmayr narrates it, saying: Ibrahim narrated from him, from his paternal aunt, from ʿAʾishah. And al-Hakim said: from ʿUmarah, from his mother, from ʿAʾishah. al-Daraqutni mentioned it in al-ʿIlal wal-Ikhtilaf and discussed the disagreement about it at length. And in the chapter there is also, from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "A Bedouin came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, my father wants to take my property. He said: You and your property belong to your father. Indeed the best that you eat is from your earnings, and the property of your children is from your earnings, so eat with ease." Related by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah through the route of al-Hajjaj ibn Arṭah from ʿAmr, and al-Hajjaj is a mudallis and there is weakness in it.]]". The meaning of ﴿from your houses﴾ is: from the houses in which your spouses and dependents are. Also, the child is closer than those relatives enumerated; so if the reason for the permission is kinship, then the one who is closer to them has more right to it. If you say: what is the meaning of ﴿or what you possess the keys to﴾? I say: when a man has over his property a supervisor and an agent who guards it for him, it is permitted for him to eat from the fruit of his orchard and drink from the milk of his livestock. And "possessing the keys" means: their being in his hand and his guarding them. It was also said: the houses of the slaves, because a slave's property belongs to his master. And it has been read: "its key" (mift*a*hahu).

If you say: what is the meaning of ﴿or your friend﴾? I say: its meaning is: or the houses of your friends. And "friend" may be singular or plural [[Mahmud said: "al-Sadiq may be singular or plural, and what is meant here is the plural." Ahmad said: al-Zamakhshari has said that the secret of its singular form in the saying of the Exalted ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any warm friend﴾, rather than "intercessors", is to draw attention to the scarcity of friends, whereas intercessors are not so, for a person may be defended and interceded for on his behalf by one who does not know him, let alone being a friend. It is possible in both verses—and Allah knows best—that the plural is meant, in which case there is no issue; and it is possible that the singular is meant, in which case that would be its secret, and Allah knows best.]], and likewise the close associate, the companion, and the enemy. It is related from al-Hasan that he entered his house and found a circle of his friends who had drawn out baskets from under his bed, containing sweet confections and fine foods, and they were bent over them eating. His face lit up with joy, he laughed, and said: "Thus we found them, thus we found them."

He meant the chief Companions and those of the Badrites whom they met, may Allah be pleased with them. A man among them would enter the house of his friend while he was absent, ask his slave-girl for his purse, and take from it whatever he wished; and when the owner of the house arrived and she informed him, he would free her out of delight at that. It is related from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with them both: Among the greatness of the sanctity of a friend is that Allah has made him, in intimacy, trust, ease, and casting off formality, equal to the self, the father, the brother, and the son. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: The friend is greater than parents; when the people of Hell cried out for help, they did not call upon fathers and mothers. Rather they said: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any warm friend﴾. And they said: when the apparent circumstance indicates the owner's consent, that stands in place of explicit permission; and asking permission may become awkward and burdensome, like someone to whom food is brought and who asks his companion's permission to eat from it.

﴿Together or separately﴾, that is, gathered or dispersed. It was revealed concerning the Banu Layth ibn ʿAmr of Kinanah, who would be scrupulous about eating alone; so a man might sit waiting all day until night, and if he found no one to eat with him, he would eat out of necessity. It was said concerning a people of the Ansar: when a guest came to them, they would not eat except with their guest. It was also said: they were scrupulous about gathering for a meal because people differ in how they eat and some exceed others. ﴿So when you enter houses﴾ from these houses in order to eat, ﴿then greet one another﴾, the ones of your own religion and kin. [[Mahmud said: "its meaning: greet the kind that is of you in religion and kinship." Ahmad said: in describing them as "yourselves" there is an allusion to the secret that required the permission to eat from these enumerated houses, and that this was because, relative to the one entering, they are like his own house, owing to the unity of kinship; so let him be content to relax there. And Allah knows best.]] ﴿a greeting from Allah﴾, that is, established by His command, prescribed by His decree.

Or, because greeting and salutation is a request for safety and life for the one greeted, and life is from Allah. Its being described as blessed and good is because it is a believer's supplication for a believer, from which increase of good and goodness of provision are hoped for from Allah. It is related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I served the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for ten years—and it is narrated: nine years—and he never said to me concerning anything I did: why did you do it? nor concerning anything I broke: why did you break it? I was standing at his head pouring water over his hands, and he raised his head and said: "Shall I teach you three qualities by which we benefit?" I said: "Yes, may my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Whenever you meet anyone of my community, greet him, and your life will be prolonged; and when you enter your house, greet its people, and the good of your house will increase; and pray the Duha prayer, for it is the prayer of the righteous who turn often [to Allah]" [[Related by Abu al-Qasim Hamzah ibn Yusuf al-Jurjani in Tarikh Jurjan, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab in the sixty-first chapter. And al-Tha'labi through the route of al-Yasaʿ ibn Zayd ibn Sahl, from Ibn ʿUtbah, from Humayd, from Anas, in full; al-Yasaʿ is the last one who claimed to have heard from Ibn ʿUtbah. He died after 280 AH and his hadith is weak; the basic hadith, apart from the story within it, is in the Sahih from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him. The rest is related from Anas through several routes. Among them is what al-Bazzar related through the route of ʿUwayd ibn ʿImran al-Jawni, from his father, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ enjoined five qualities upon me. He said: Perform wudu thoroughly, it will increase your life; greet whoever of my community you meet, your good deeds will multiply; when you enter your house, greet your family, the good of your house will increase; and pray the Duha prayer, for it is the prayer of the ones who turn often; and show mercy to the young and honour the elderly, and you will be among my companions." ʿUwayd: Ibn Hibban said: he narrates from his father what is not from his hadith. Abu Yaʿla related it through the narration of ʿAmr ibn Abi Khalifah from Dirar ibn ʿAmr from Anas, and its chain is very weak. Likewise al-Tabarani in al-Saghir related it through ʿAmr ibn Dinar from Anas, and its narrator from him is discarded. al-ʿUqayli related it through al-Fadl ibn al-ʿAbbas from Thabit from Anas, and al-Fadl is unknown. Al-ʿUqayli said: no one follows him in it except one who is weaker than him or prior to him. Ibn ʿAdi related it through Azwar ibn Ghalib from Sulayman al-Taymi from Anas. Ibn Tahir said: Azwar is a rejected narrator. It has another route from Anas which is weaker than these.]]." And they said:

If there is no one in the house, let him say: "Peace be upon us from our Lord; peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah. Peace be upon the people of the house and the mercy of Allah." And from Ibn ʿAbbas: when you enter the mosque, say: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," a greeting from Allah. ﴿A greeting﴾ is governed by "greet", because it is in the sense of "a salutation", like your saying: "I sat, a sitting."

Almighty and Majestic is He wanted to show them the gravity of the offence in one who departs from the gathering of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ without his permission, when they are with him on a matter that brings people together. So He made not departing until they seek his permission the third of faith in Allah and faith in His Messenger, and made the two of them like the prelude of a love poem (tashbib) [[His saying "and made the two of them like the tashbib for him": in al-Sihah, tashbib is al-nasib (the amorous prelude), as one says "he performs tashbib with so-and-so," meaning he speaks amorously of her (a)]] and the preamble to mention of him. This is together with opening the sentence with innama ("only") and placing the believers as the subject, with a relative clause as its predicate whose complement encompasses the mention of the two faiths. Then he followed it with what increases it in emphasis and intensity, where he repeated it in another style, namely His saying ﴿Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾, and he included in it another thing: that He made seeking permission like the proof of the soundness of the two faiths, and He alluded to the state of the hypocrites and their slipping away secretly.

The meaning of His saying ﴿they do not leave until they seek his permission﴾ is: they do not leave until they seek his permission and he grants it to them. Do you not see how He made the command, after their seeking permission exists, dependent on his will and his permission to whomever he deems fitting to grant it to? The "matter that brings together" (al-amr al-jami') is that for which people are gathered. The matter is described as "gathering" by way of metaphor, such as fighting an enemy, consulting about an important affair, banding together to terrify an opponent, or pledging mutual support in an alliance, and other things. Or it is a matter whose harm or benefit is general. It was also read as amr jami' (a matter of gathering). In His saying ﴿when they are with him on a matter that brings together﴾ there is an indication that it is a grave affair in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ must have people of opinion and strength who back him, assist him, and benefit from their opinions, knowledge, and experience in what suffices him. So the departure of one of them in such a situation is burdensome to his heart and disturbs his judgment. For this reason He was strict with them and restricted the matter of seeking permission, despite the extended excuse and the pressing need for it and the occurrence of what concerns and affects them. This is His saying ﴿for some of their affairs﴾.

The mention of seeking forgiveness for those who ask permission is evidence that the better and more excellent course is that they should not entertain in themselves the thought of leaving, nor seek permission for it. It was said: it was revealed concerning the digging of the trench, when some people were slipping away without permission. They said: "Thus should people be with their imams and leaders in religion and knowledge, supporting them and not forsaking them in any calamity of calamities, and not scattering away from them." As for permission, the matter is delegated to the imam: if he wills he grants permission, and if he wills he does not grant it, according to what his judgment requires.

If the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) needs your gathering before him for a matter and calls you, then do not disperse from him except with his permission. And do not equate his calling you with one another's calling, nor your leaving the assembly without the permission of the one who calls.

Or: do not make his naming and calling among you like one of you naming and calling another, by the name his parents gave him. Do not say, "O Muhammad," but say, "O Prophet of Allah," or "O Messenger of Allah," with reverence, veneration, a lowered voice, and humility. It is also possible that the meaning is: do not make the Messenger's supplication to his Lord like your young asking your old, or your poor asking your rich, for a need, which is sometimes granted and sometimes refused. For the supplications of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are heard and answered.

﴿يَتَسَلَّلُونَ﴾ means they slip away little by little. The equivalent of tasallala (to slip away stealthily) is tadarraja (to proceed gradually) and tadakhkhala (to slip in). As for liwādh (furtive hiding behind one another): it is mulāwadha, which is that one person hides behind another and the other behind him, meaning they slip away from the congregation secretly, in the manner of mulāwadha, each concealing himself behind the others. The word liwādhan is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), meaning: "hiding behind one another." It has also been said: some of them would hide behind a man when he asked permission, and he would grant it to him, and then the one who had not been given permission would leave along with him.

It is recited as "law idhā" with a fatḥah (the particle lawā / lawa with idhā). It is said: khālafahu ilā al-amr (he went to the matter without him), meaning he went to it apart from him. From this is the words of Allah, ﴿وَما أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُخالِفَكُمْ إِلى ما أَنْهاكُمْ عَنْهُ﴾ ("And I do not intend to go against you in what I forbid you"). And khālafahu 'an al-amr: when he turns away from it without him, meaning he deviates from it. The meaning of ﴿الَّذِينَ يُخالِفُونَ عَنْ أَمْرِهِ﴾ ("those who oppose His command") is those who turn away from his command, apart from the believers, and they are the hypocrites. The object has been omitted because the purpose is to mention the one who opposes and the one opposed.

The pronoun in amrihi ("His command") refers to Allah, the Exalted, or to the Messenger (ﷺ). The meaning is: from his obedience and his religion. ﴿فِتْنَةٌ﴾ means a trial in this world, ﴿أَوْ يُصِيبَهُمْ عَذابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ means a painful punishment in the Hereafter. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that fitnah means killing. It is reported from 'Ata' that it means earthquakes and terrors. It is reported from Ja'far ibn Muhammad that it means a cruel ruler will be set over them.

أدخل (قد) ليؤكد علمه بما هم عليه من المخالفة عن الدين والنفاق ومرجع توكيد العلم إلى توكيد الوعيد، وذلك أن (قد) إذا دخلت على المضارع كانت بمعنى «ربما» فوافقت «ربما» في خروجها إلى معنى التكثير في نحو قوله:

*Qad* (قد) was introduced to emphasize His knowledge of their deviation from the religion and their hypocrisy. The emphasis on knowledge returns to the emphasis on the threat. This is because *qad* (قد), when it precedes the present-tense verb, carries the meaning of *rubba* (ربما, "perhaps" or "often"), and it agrees with *rubba* in moving toward the sense of multiplicity, as in the verse:

فان تمس مهجور الفناء فربّما ... أقام به بعد الوفود وفود [[ألا إن عينا لم تجد يوم واسط ... عليك يجارى دمعها لجمود

عشية قام النائحات وشققت ... جيوب بأيدى مأتم وخدود

فان تمس مهجور الفناء فربما ... أقام به بعد الوفود وفود

لابن عطاء السندي: يرث ى ابن هبيرة لما قتله المنصور. وواسط: موضع الواقعة. وأتم بالمكان: أقام به.

والمأتم: مكان الاقامة: استعمل في جماعة النساء الحزينات مجازا مشهورا، وجمعه: مآتم بمد الهمزة. يقول:

إن كل عين لم تبك عليك ذلك اليوم لشديدة الجمود. وعشية: بدل من يوم. وجيب القميص. مخرج الرأس منه، أى: مزقت الجيوب والخدود بأيدى النساء، ثم التفت إلى الخطاب، وصبر وتصبر بقوله: فان تمس مهجور الفناء، كناية عن الموت، فربما: أى كثيرا أقام بفناء بيتك جموع من الناس بعد جموع، يستمنحونك، أى: فان يهجر فناؤك الآن فلا حزن، لأنه كثيرا ما اجتمع فيه الناس ومنحوا خيرا.]]

Translation of the verse: "If your courtyard is left deserted, then surely many a host has camped in it after host." Here "*majaz*" (مجاز, figurative usage) and "*kināya*" (كناية, allusion or metonymy) are used as technical terms.

The poem is by Ibn ʿAṭāʾ al-Sindī, lamenting Ibn Hubayra when al-Mansur killed him. Wasit is the site of the battle. The verb *atam bi-l-makān* (أتم بالمكان) means "he stayed in the place." *Al-ma'tam* (المأتم) means the place of residence, and by a well-known figurative usage it is applied to the group of grieving women. Its plural is *ma'ātim* (مآتم) with a lengthened *alif*. The poet says: Every eye that did not weep for you on that day is indeed very hard in its tears. *ʿAshiyya* (عشية) is in apposition to *yawm* (يوم). *Jayb* (جيب) is the opening of a shirt through which the head passes; the meaning is that the collars and cheeks were torn by the hands of the women. Then he turned to address the one being addressed, and consoled and comforted him by saying: "If your courtyard is left deserted," which is a metaphor (*kināya*) for death. "*Fa-rubba*" (فربما) means: many a host of people came to camp at the courtyard of your house, one host after another, seeking your generosity. In other words, even if your courtyard is now left deserted, there is no cause for grief, because people had often gathered there and been granted good.

ونحوه قول زهير:

أخى ثقة لا تهلك الخمر ماله ... ولكنّه قد يهلك المال نائله [[تقدم شرح هذا الشاهد بالجزء الثاني صفحة 17 فراجعه إن شئت اه مصححه.]]

Similar is the verse of Zuhayr:

"My brother is trustworthy; wine does not destroy his wealth, but rather his giving may destroy the wealth."

والمعنى. أنّ جميع ما في السموات والأرض مختصة به خلقا وملكا وعلما، فكيف يخفى عليه أحوال المنافقين وإن كانوا يجتهدون في سترها عن العيون وإخفائها. وسينبئهم يوم القيامة بما أبطنوا من سوء أعمالهم وسيجازيهم حق جزائهم. والخطاب والغيبة في قوله ﴿قَدْ يَعْلَمُ ما أَنْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ وَيَوْمَ يُرْجَعُونَ إِلَيْهِ﴾ يجوز أن يكونا جميعا المنافقين على طريق الالتفات. ويجوز أن يكون (ما أنتم عليه) عاما، و (يرجعون) للمنافقين، والله أعلم.

The meaning: All that is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him in creation, dominion, and knowledge. How, then, could the conditions of the hypocrites be hidden from Him, even though they strive to conceal them from eyes and to hide them? "And He will inform them on the Day of Resurrection of what they concealed of their evil deeds, and He will recompense them their due recompense." The second-person address and third-person reference in His words, ﴿He knows what you are upon, and the Day they are returned to Him﴾, may both refer to the hypocrites by way of *iltifāt* (التفات, a shift in grammatical person within a discourse). It is also permissible that "what you are upon" is general, and "they are returned" refers to the hypocrites. And God knows best.

عن رسول الله ﷺ: «من قرأ سورة النور أعطى من الأجر عشر حسنات بعدد كل مؤمن ومؤمنة فيما مضى وفيما بقي [[أخرجه الثعلبي وابن مردويه باسناديهما إلى أبى بن كعب رضى الله عنه.]] » .

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Nur will be given the reward of ten good deeds for each believing man and believing woman, in the past and in what remains."
